speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
subtopic: TABLING OP REGULATIONS GOVERNING TEMPORARY VISITS AND TRANSITIONAL PASSAGE
speechtext:
I desire to lay on the table copy of an order in council passed on May 5 affecting the movement of Chinese into Canada and out of Canada. The house will recall that on April 17 the Prime Minister informed the house that a draft immigration treaty with China was under consideration which would establish on a mutual and reciprocal basis the admission to each country of approved categories of persons from the other. Pending the bringing into effect of this treaty the order in council, which is No. P.C. 3378, has been passed. It covers Chinese persons wishing to pass through Canada in transit to another place, and also Chinese persons who wish to come here for temporary visits. Henceforth the persons involved will be dealt with under the ordinary provisions of the Immigration Act. In addition, the order modifies some provisions which hitherto restricted the position of Chinese residents in Canada who wished to go outside the country for a visit and subsequently return.
I might add that the order in council changes only the regulations governing temporary visits and "in transit" passage, and does not affect the provisions governing entry to Canada for permanent residence. These have been left for settlement in the treaty negotiations of which the Prime Minister spoke.

subtopic: REMOVAL FROM TRAIN PROCEEDING TO CANADA FROM THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Arising out of the statement which the minister has just made, I desire to 100-182
ask whether he has seen the latest issue of the New Republic, which renews the controversy with respect to a girl of Chinese origin who was taken off a train at Buffalo. I understand that the question is now put up squarely to the government-not perhaps that the person involved in the commission of this act was a Canadian; the statement of the Prime Minister and of the minister in that respect apparently is correct-but the point now raised is that it was done in accordance with Canadian law. For the most part the cabinet is engaged with it and it is hard to get a copy. May I say that everyone will be in agreement that we should not discourage in any way other nations from praising our war effort, so far as the Canadian people are concerned. I think there will be general unanimity in the house on that point. Our real problem, however, amounts to this, and it is a very simple one, particularly in a year when perhaps, with the heat of elections that are approaching, it is very difficult at times to distinguish between praising of the Canadian people's war effort and praise of the effort of members of a one-party government and its Prime Minister who is running the war at the present moment.

Mr. Speaker, we may as well be frank about this. There is no desire to be acrimonious on the point at all, but when the leader of the government makes the statement he does, I think it is well to put this on the record, because so far as we are concerned-
You are ashamed.

Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to finish at any rate. The fact is that in all these things which have arisen from time to time, such as this, it is well for Mr. Winchell and other gentlemen in the United States, and in other countries as well, to know that it has all stemmed not from what they honestly think and say with respect to the domestic situation here, but from the fact that rightly or wrongly, and I think wrongly, the Canadian war effort, because the government has so decided, has been run by a one-party administration. These things stem of course from that cause.

I think I have a right to say a word on that. My hon. friend has put his finger right on it. If it is going to be regarded as a cardinal principle that we cannot have any praise of Canada's war effort for fear it might possibly enure to the benefit or the credit of the administration, then it has come to a sad pass in this country. If my hon. friend and the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), as well as the hon. gentleman who asked this question, are so thin-skinned about it, then it seems to me it indicates perhaps that they have not a proper appreciation of the responsibilities of public men.
Thanks for the lecture.

I happen to have in my hand the statement which was made by Mr. Winchell. I had not seen it before, but I have glanced through it. There is not one sentence in it which by the wildest stretch of the imagination could be regarded as giving credit to any particular government. As my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) has said, the whole statement is with regard to the effort of the Canadian people.
I think my hon. friend will join with me in this. I think we would feel very badly if we happened to praise the United States' war effort, happening to come as it does under the administration of President Roosevelt, and then found ourselves pilloried by questions in the Congressional Record asking whether or not we were in the pay of the United States

government or the United States administration. That is the imputation that is cast on Mr. Winchell, and that is the imputation that my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources properly undertook to refute in the statement that he made.

I can hardly think that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ralston) was attempting to indicate that so far as we were concerned there was a desire on the part of any of us to prevent discussion or a description of Canada's war effort. I think I made it clear at the beginning that I had not seen the article, and more than that if it were the kind of article that is sometimes put out giving praise not to the Canadian people but to others, then there is justification for criticism on that score. I do not think we are very far apart in this matter, but I do think when it is remembered that we have a one-party administration it is obvious that these questions will crop up. It is difficult at times to avoid them.
All I can say is there appeared to be an attempt to question the good faith and accuracy of statements made by a gentleman in commendation of Canada's war effort. That was the desire.
We did not suggest any such thing.
Has this not gone on long enough?

The United States military authorities have not opened an office in Vancouver, B.C., to recruit labour for the Alaska highway. The United States authorities have, however, maintained an accounts office in Vancouver for the past eighteen months.
The accounts office referred to is not attempting to hire men in Vancouver for the Alaska highway and no, requests for men to work on this highway have been placed with the national selective service office at Vancouver.
The Standard Oil company placed an order for seventy-five men for the Canol Oil Refinery project, which was later reduced to eight men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 12, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Administration of the defence of Canada regulations, $30,000.

I should like the Minister of Justice to give the committee a review of the general principles now applicable in reference to the release of men from internment camps. Considerable agitation has been aroused in this country by the recent release of three men named Joseph Farr, John Lorimer and Alois N. Schneider. I do not know very much about the first two, who I understand were incarcerated because of their fascist leaning, but I do know something about the last named, who comes from Saskatchewan. I understand that these men were interned because they were believed to be in sympathy with the German reieh. If that was the reason for their internment, I suggest that conditions have not altered sufficiently to justify the administration in concluding that they now should be released.
This man Schneider, who lives in the northern part of Saskatchewan, was interned on September 5, 1939; he was picked up by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, presumably because they had information that he was the type of man likely to be dangerous in time of war. Subsequently, after considerable pressure had been brought to bear, he was released on December 21, 1939. I may add that the information in connection with this matter is contained in a question asked by myself and answered by the minister on May 4 of this year, and appearing in Hansard of that date. This man Schneider was out of the internment camp from December 21, 1939, to June 10, 1940, when he was again incarcerated. According to an answer given me by the minister to-day, he was placed in the internment camp on the second occasion for this reason:
The war situation in Europe and the general apprehension of possible subversive (fifth column) activities extending to Canada.
I should like to know whether the minister and the administration believe the situation to be any less tense to-day, so far as Europe is concerned, than it was at that time, and whether or not there is now reason for less

War Appropriation-Justice

general apprehension in respect to possible subversive fifth column activities. This man was returned to the internment camp on June 10, 1940, and remained there until February 21, 1944, when he was released. According to the information I received to-day in answer to another question, he was released after making three applications. The first was made on September 23, 1939, and after a hearing on December 4, 1939, no recommendation was made by the committee. However, as I mentioned a moment ago, he was released some seventeen days later, apparently solely on the responsibility of the administration. On July 9, 1942, he applied again for release; his hearing was on September 22, 1942, and the recommendation of the committee was that he should be continued in detention. On October 16, 1943, he made another application, which was heard about February 16, 1944, and he was granted his conditional release. The question I asked on May 4, as to the reason for his release on the previous occasion, was as follows:
What change has there been in the conditions with respect to this man since the date of his reinternment which would justify his release ?
The answer was:
The information which was before the advisory committee must be treated as confidential, but in addition to that which concerned Alois N. Schneider himself, it was publicly known that he has two nephews in the Canadian army overseas, and his own son, who is not old enough to join the army, is serving in the home defence force.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not know what difference it makes whether a man has nephews in the army, or even whether he has a son in the reserve army. If this man was placed in an internment camp because he was a danger to Canada through his sympathies with the German reich, conditions have not altered in the meantime, I suggest, to the extent indicated by the minister in his answer to these questions. The point is that if this man was properly placed in an internment camp in the first place, in my judgment conditions have not changed sufficiently to justify his release at the present time. If he was improperly placed in the internment camp in the first place, then the administration should be frank with this house and advise us that the man never should have been put in the camp. If that is the proper answer, an explanation should be given as to why he was allowed to remain there for this length of time.
I understand that the same situation exists with respect to the other two men I have mentioned, though I do not know very much

about them and am not prepared to debate the point. It seems to me that if this man Schneider was properly interned in the first place because of his sympathy with the German reich, a better explanation than has been given by the minister should be advanced to this house for his release at the present time. It may be that he promised to be a good boy; I do not know. It was suggested in the press the other day that Mr. Camillien Houde might be released from internment if in effect he would promise to be a good boy, and I am just wondering if this is why Mr. Schneider and these other so-called fascists were released, if they have now promised not to do any harm as far as our war effort is concerned.

I should like to say a word about this man Alois N. Schneider, because he happens to live in a town in my constituency. As hon. members know, he was arrested in 1939; then, for what reason we do not know, he was released. I have tried to ascertain from the minister who was responsible for getting him released, but unfortunately I have been unable to get this information.
Do you know what date he was released?

In December, 1939, I believe.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Would it be possible, Mr. Chairman, for us at this end of the chamber to have some part in this discussion of my estimates?

May I proceed, Mr. Chairman? The facts are well known, and I am afraid they are not going to be very welcome to hon. members who sit on the opposite benches. While the Minister of Justice did not tell this house who was responsible for obtaining the release of this man Schneider, people up in the northern part of the country know very well that his release was desired very greatly by the former Liberal member of the house, whom I happened to defeat, Mr. McIntosh, whose organizer he was up in that northern area.
I must say that up in the northern part of my country we have a number of German people, and I believe their position during this war has been very terrible.
Many of them had relatives still at home in Germany. Before the war began these people used to receive letters from their relatives telling them that things in Germany were much better, that there was no depression over there, that they did not have unemployment, and that Hitler was building roads and making employment. They were told that

War Appropriation

Justice
this, that and the other thing was good. I can remember talking to one of these German people on the street of a small town up north. He said to me, "Look at our little town, with all these youngsters standing around the pool parlours, with nothing to do. It is not that way in Germany. We have clubs; we have the youth movement for our children." I can quite understand a person like Mr. Schneider, who was in a position to prey upon the fears of these German people, naturally reaching the point where he would be looked upon by them as a leader. There is no doubt whatsoever that he was nazi in his sympathies, and that he tried to organize in that direction. Then, this man Schneider happened to be land agent and machine agent, and possibly to many of these people he had become a friend. He might allow them a little more time for payment on land, or might make a good deal with them for machinery. *
Was he a government employee?

I do not think he was. But possibly he was in a position where he had a hold over them. Then when he suggested that they join the bund, it is possible that they would agree with him, and in this way he would build up an organization in that part of the country.
But the great majority of these German farmers were very poor, with little time to think about politics. All they wanted to do was to get a living from the land, and be ordinary, good Canadian people. I know that. As soon as the war started there was a certain amount of hysteria among some people. Indeed, anyone who had a German name had to be very careful what he said. Many selfappointed vigilante committees were set up here and there, and if anyone with a German name happened to say anything that sounded suspicious he would be reported by the committee. I think a number of German people were arrested at the beginning of the war without any real cause. I had a conversation with the minister's deputy-I refer to Mr. Anderson, the gentleman who now sits in front of him-regarding the release of one of these Germans in my part of the country. This was a young man named Zieglansburger, who had been arrested and interned. I feel certain that inadvertently he had said something that was picked up and reported, but I am just as certain that he had no use whatsoever for the nazi ideology. However, he was a German, and people in that state of hysteria felt that every German should be arrested and put away. I am not in sympathy with that. Many of our German people have no desire other than that of being good 100-183J
Canadians. But when we find a man like Schneider, who was definitely organizing those with whom he came in contact under the nazi doctrine, we must place him in a very different category from the ordinary run of German farmer. I repeat that we should know whether this man has been wrongfully interned for a period of some years. If so, why is it that we have not had his release before this? If he was just a poor, innocent person whose German name was responsible for his internment, we should know it. If on the other hand he was picked up twice, once in 1939 and again in 1940, there must have been some reason for it. And if those reasons justified his internment until now, why was he released just a few weeks before a provincial election?
I have no doubt at all that this man is very busy, working in an organizational capacity for the Liberal party in that part of the country. I say this emphatically, because I believe the people of that north country should be given the facts, and I say the committee would be justified in having from the minister a much more comprehensive statement than we have had in the past respecting this man's activities.

Mr. Chairman, in days gone by I have been somewhat instrumental in advocating in the house that Canada should set an example to the rest of the world in respect of its attitude in standing for freedom of religion and freedom of worship. In this respect I wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice upon the lifting of the ban from Jehovah's Witnesses some time ago. I believe that was a proper course to take, and that by so doing he has exemplified to the rest of the world the fact that we do give to every individual the right to worship God as he chooses. However, there is another matter I should like to bring before the minister. I would ask him to consider what is done with certain members of the sect known as Jehovah's Witnesses when they refuse to take up arms. I think many hon. members have had correspondence similar to what I received the other day. I might explain, however, that that which I received has to do with certain members of Jehovah's Witnesses who had been taken into custody because they refused to take up arms. The correspondence enclosed certain sworn affidavits from interested people -perhaps other members of the same organization who had visited these men while in detention-and I believe these sworn statements will give some idea of how these men have been treated.
It is my intention to read certain paragraphs from these affidavits, and I appeal to the minister to do what he can in the matter.
War Appropriation

Justice

After all, we do want to see justice done in Canada. I shall not read the technical or legal part of this document, but only those paragraphs in which the statements are made. The following is from an affidavit signed by Elva F. Patzer of the city of Winnipeg.
I do solemnly declare that:
1.	On Sunday, April 23, 1944, I attended at the detention barracks at Fort Osborne barracks in M.D. No. 10 and there in the presence of a guard did interview my brother, Gordon Mark Morrow, above named who is there held in detention, undergoing ninety days detention, because of his conscientious objections to doing military service.
2.	At the time his face was swollen, and one hand was bruised across the back of the wrist.
3.	My said brother informed me that three members of the army had previously struck him with their sticks behind the ears, on his hands and wrists, and that they had in addition struck him with their fists.
4.	My said brother also informed me that previously some soldiers tied a loaded pack on his back, which was secured by a rope fastened around his throat, that he was then violently pushed around, and the rope cut off his breath. That he also had been abused by soldiers, who picked him up and threw him violently to the floor and then jumped on him with their knees. He afterwards complained of internal pain which bothered him greatly, and he believed that he had a broken rib or ribs.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is' of the same force and effect as if made under oath by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
Declared before me. . .
And so on. This is signed by E. F. Patzer, and by J. F. Davidson, a barrister at law.
Then, there is another affidavit concerning another of these men-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member says he has another such affidavit. I wonder if he is under the impression that this has anything to do with the defence of Canada regulations. As I understand from the affidavit the hon. member read, the declarer attended at a military detention camp and received certain information from a person detained there. The Department of Justice has nothing to do with the administration of military district No 10 or of any other military district. If this affidavit covers something which arose in a detention camp of the army there would be nothing under the defence of Canada regulations which my department could do about it. There is nothing under those regulations to justify the maltreatment of any person.

I am sorry if I brought this up under the wrong department. Now that the minister draws it to my attention I believe he is right. When these men are picked up and interned they come under the Department of National Defence?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would assume that they would be men who were called up under the mobilization regulations administered by the Department of' Labour. After that they would appear before a board and would be either postponed or turned over to the military authorities, if they came within the regulations. At no stage would they be dealt with under the defence of Canada regulations.

Mr. Chairman-*
Mr.. HANSELL: I am not quite through.
I am trying to help the hon. member if he will allow me.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Macleod has the floor.

I should be pleased if the hon. member for York-Sunbury would help me out after I have finished. If what the minister has said is true, then the matter may have to be brought up under the Department of National Defence. I will not read the other affidavit; it is similar to the one I have read, but applies to another person.
I know that the minister does not want this sort of thing happening within military camps, even though it does not come under his department. All I ask him to do under the circumstances is to appeal to the Minister of National Defence to have this sort of thing stopped. It does not make any difference under what department it may come; it is not justice to persecute a man by physical torture because of his particular religious convictions. I appeal to the Minister of Justice to bring this thing to the attention of the Minister of National Defence and have it stopped immediately.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the committee, but first I should like to congratulate the minister upon having lifted the ban against those citizens who call themselves Jehovah's Witnesses. I think they are very sincere, but in my opinion they are on the wrong track. I was going to say something else, but I shall not. I think that action came a little late because there was a great deal of persecution, not prosecution, of these misguided people. I believe the minister is correct in suggesting that the cases before the committee are those of conscientious objectors who are under detention because of their unwillingness to serve in the army after having been drafted or called.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Or to take alternate service.

War Appropriation-Justice

Or to take alternate service, as we know is the case. I received two of these affidavits to-day and I read .them with a good deal of astonishment. I just cannot believe that these things can be true in Canada in this twentieth century. I may say to the minister that in law these affidavits are only hearsay evidence. They are not the affidavits of the persons detained; they are affidavits of those who interviewed the persons in the detention camp. As the lawyers say, that is hearsay, but inasmuch they have made these declarations on information and belief-that is the way we put it as lawyers-they call for some explanation on the part of the authorities, by way of refutation or investigation.
I should like to read one paragraph of one of these declarations, and then I am going to ask the minister to do what the hon. member for Macleod asked him to do. This is an affidavit by Stephie Klymuik, of Whyte-wold, Manitoba, being a declaration under the Canada Evidence Act. She visited a man by the name of Adam Remando at the detention barracks at Fort Osborne, military district No. 10, on April 16. The following is not his statement; it is what the declarer says was told to her, and she passes it on by way of opinion and presumably belief. The paragraph reads:
Remando then informed me he had been put on a bread and water diet for refusing to put on the ' uniform, that his clothes had been violently torn from him and destroyed, and he was forcibly dressed in a uniform and ordered to pick up a gun, which he refused to do.
Mark this:
That he was beaten and badly injured and put under an ice cold shower for twenty minutes, and that later on a gun was tied to his arm for several days.
I can scarcely believe that that took place in Canada, It sounds like what would happen under a third degree in New York where Mr. Walter Winchell comes from, the gentleman we heard about this afternoon. That is what they do down there under third degree, but surely it does not happen in Canada. I am going to ask the minister to call the attention of the Minister of National Defence to these allegations. If they are true, then third degree methods are being adopted by the army to force men into the home army. That is what it means. No matter how much we may object to conscientious objectors not doing their duty as citizens as we see it, I do not believe the people of Canada will for one moment tolerate this sort of treatment. I am going to give the department the benefit of the doubt to which they are entitled- this evidence does not comply with the best evidence rule.
These people are people whom we want to make into good Canadians if we can. They have been invited to this country. I presume they came here lawfully, that they had lawful entry. They are not criminals. For their conscience' sake they may be ready to undergo punishment, but certainly they should not have to suffer this punishment, if it is true as charged. Will the minister tell us upon what date the prohibition against Jehovah's Witnesses was lifted, how many prosecutions there were under the defence of Canada regulations, and where they were?

May I say that the
first of these two cases is not new either to my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or to myself. We got the first affidavit some few weeks ago, and because we though? the situation warranted it, the allegations being so grave, we turned it over to the Minister of National Defence. The second affidavit was treated similarly. Immediately I received it I sent it by messenger to the minister. I know that in the first instance some investigation has already taken place. Since this matter has been raised this afternoon, if the investigations have been completed the Minister of National Defence might inform the house what the situation is in this regard. I share the view of the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for York-Sunbury that if these allegations are true they are an exceedingly grave reflection on our country.
They are shocking.

-and upon the administration of. justice in this country. They should be thoroughly probed by the department and a report made to this house, and there should be no sort of inquiry held in secret. Charges as serious as these having been made in this house and read into the record, they should be dealt with openly and an inquiry held, with all the evidence taken, and the various parties to it provided with proper counsel.
In the presence of the subject and his counsel if he so wishes.
That is what I mean. We presented this case 'to the Minister of National Defence some days ago. I see he is in his seat now, and I think it would be wise if he made a statement to the committee.

I was just informed that there had been brought up in committee the matter of the treatment of a certain number of men belonging to the sect known as Jehovah's Witnesses, in Winnipeg. I am a little surprised that it should be brought up
War Appropriation-Justice

on this particular item under the Department of Justice, because it is a matter for the army and under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence. I understand that affidavits have been read-*
Statutory declarations.
-which I have not heard.
I will send them over.
I assume they are the affidavits which I myself received; and as I remember, all the affidavits are by somebody who said he was told by somebody else-
They are hearsay; I made that clear.
-that certain things took place. I received a wire with regard to it from a relative of a man whose name, I think, is Morrow-
That is right.
In view of the seriousness of these charges-we have had three of them recently, one at Windsor and two from Winnipeg
I did not hear of two from Winnipeg.
Yes, two from Winnipeg, I think.
There are four men. My hon. friend means, the same group?
The same group of people, yes.
I want to be sure what my hon. friend says. I am treating as one group the charges with regard to these four men.

There are two separate persons, and there was the case at Windsor. I do not know how these courts of inquiry are conducted, whether the military-

War Appropriation-Justice

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I should have taken up the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice. I realize how difficult it is for members of the committee and for myself to make distinctions between different departments, because at times the margin seems to be narrow. But although the statement which has just been made by the Minister of National Defence comes under his department, I think hon. members should remain within the orbit of the item before the committee; otherwise we shall never get anywhere. There will be other opportunities to discuss this matter, when the proper department is before the committee of the whole.

I do not want to disagree with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I was just going to say something which I think should be said now; and may I suggest that technically I have the right to discuss anything which appears in these war appropriation estimates-anything. We have passed nothing. This is no bill with a schedule; we are dealing with a resolution. I can pick up this resolution at any point and deal with any department I wish, under the rules of this house. That is one of the reasons why, when this appropriation was coming down, I suggested it would facilitate business if we could have a bill and a schedule attached to the bill. I do not want to depart from any understanding we may have reached as to dealing with this resolution, but technically I would be well within my rights even though I spent the whole afternoon discussing subjects other than those pertaining to the Department of Justice.
I hope my hon. friend is not invoking that, because there is an agreement as to the way we shall proceed.

I am talking of my right. I suggest to the minister that, in view of the nature of these charges, if these courts are held in secret, he would be well advised to have an open inquiry into these cases in order that all parties can be satisfied. I am not questioning in any way the integrity of the court of inquiry; I am suggesting to the minister that in the public interest and the interest of the department it would be well to consider the point I have raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the point brought by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I know that he would be the last hon. member not to realize what is, I am sure, understood by the committee, that when a minister and
his officials attend on behalf of a particular department, it is understood that we will remain within the limits of that department.
I know that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will realize that it is impossible to have two or three ministers and half a dozen or more officials waiting around all the time, on one particular item.

I had not intended to discuss the question which has just been brought up. I am not a member of Jehovah's Witnesses. There has been a good deal of discussion of the real reason why they were banned, and I think the Minister of Justice should make a statement on the matter which would satisfy the curiosity of the country.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I cannot satisfy the hon. member on that point. When I became Minister of Justice I found certain defence of Canada regulations which had been adopted by the governor in council, and which had been before a committee of the house and had been approved thereby. I had no choice but to apply them until such time as they were modified, and on recommendation I made in October, 1943, the ban was lifted.

How many prosecutions had taken place against Jehovah's Witnesses up to that period?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There had been no prosecutions by the Department of Justice against Jehovah's Witnesses up to that period. Such prosecutions as had been instituted had been instituted by the attorneys general of the provinces or under their control, applying the defence of Canada regulations as part of the law of Canada.

How many had been carried out at the instigation of the Department of Justice?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No prosecutions had been instituted at the instigation of the department against any persons for being members of Jehovah's Witnesses.

May I ask whether all restrictions imposed upon Jehovah's Witnesses have been lifted, or whether only the right to meet at their services has been restored?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Some time over a year ago there had been a modification of the regulations to the effect that no one would commit an offence by attending a meeting for the purpose of religious worship. In October, 1943, regulation 39(c) was amended by striking therefrom the names of "the
War Appropriation-Justice

following organizations", and among them was the name of Jehovah's Witnesses. So that section 39(c) no longer applies in any way to the persons known as Jehovah's Witnesses.

Jehovah's Witnesses
have a number of subsidiary organizations such as the Watch Tower publishing company and some others. I have been informed that the literature of the organization is still banned. I have also been told-I was going to try to verify this before, but since the matter is now under consideration I will mention it, without any definite knowledge of the question -that all literature emanating from the Watch Tower publishing company is automatically banned from Canada, and that on one occasion not long ago a shipment of Holy Bibles, the King James authorized version, was prohibited from entering this country simply because these bibles bore the name of the publisher. I was told that there was no commentary, nothing but the King James authorized edition of the bible, published by the Watch Tower publishing company, and because it was published by this organization the shipment was prohibited. I do not know whether that is true. Is it true?
That is correct, yes.
Were they imported from London?
No; from the United States.

The minister says it is true. I think there should be an easement of that provision at once. I do not think anything should be allowed to interfere with the importation of the Holy Bible into this country, even when it is published by the Watch Tower publishing company. I cannot see that it would interfere with the war effort of the country or undermine the principles of any of our people, to have the bible brought into the country even when it bears the imprint	of any publishing	house,	which
happens to be in this intance the Watch Tower company.

The money goes to a prohibited organization. That is the reason.
Mr.	COLDWELL:	The	ban	against
Jehovah's Witnesses-

I am speaking of the
Watch Tower publishing company.
Mr.	COLDWELL:	The	ban	againstJehovah's Witnesses is	lifted.	If the	parent
organization is legal, why should a subsidiary be considered illegal and prohibited?

The defence of Canada regulations committee two years ago recommended lifting the ban from Jehovah's Witnesses and that included the subsidiary organizations referred to, the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, and some others. The ban was lifted from Jehovah's Witnesses but not from these societies or organizations through which Jehovah's Witnesses hold their property. This situation exists in my city, where Jehovah's Witnesses as individuals, through the medium of an incorporated society which is banned, own a hall. They are forced into the position where they must go and rent, from the custodian of enemy property, the very hall which they themselves bought with their own money through the medium of this organization which is still banned. I suggest that the administration ought to reconsider the position, because it leaves the matter in an anomalous state. As a matter of fact, first of all, the custodian refused to rent to these Jehovah's Witnesses, though eventually he did. I suggest that the halls should be returned to those who put their money into them.

This whole subject
becomes very much involved when one digs deep into it. It might be supposed that because the Minister of Justice has lifted the ban from Jehovah's Witnesses, therefore they should be allowed to go around and do-whatever they wish. I do not agree with that position. I am not speaking for my group, because this is not a party matter. It is a matter of what appeals to one's own intelligence and common sense. I can quite understand that the ban might be lifted from a religious organization for the purpose of giving them the right of freedom of worship, and yet it might not be lifted from a certain publication which might teach things that are contrary to peace, order and good government. I was tempted to ask, when the member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke about bibles, whether there were any comments on them.
None.

I am told that the funds were to be paid to an organization that is still under the ban. I fancy that means that if the Jehovah's Witnesses had ordered bibles from some other publishing house those bibles would have come in all right. That, I suppose, would be the answer. I sympathize with the minister to this extent, that it is difficult to draw the line between what might constitute freedom of worship and what might be taught in certain religious meetings. I believe that people should be free to assemble and worship God according to their conscience.

The scriptures, of course, are subject to a variety of interpretations. My interpretation is that the scriptures teach that we must be subject to the powers that are ordained of God to rule the nations. You cannot very well say, "I will disobey the law of the land," and at the same time say, "I will obey the law of God"; because to my mind to obey God is to obey a law of the land. It is an exacting position. I am an advocate of lifting the ban on Jehovah's Witnesses. I am a great advocate of freedom of worship, but I am not an advocate of permitting anyone to go and do and teach whatever they wish. They may teach truth and truth alone. There again you come up against this difficulty: what one may regard as truth in the bible may not be regarded as a proper interpretation by someone else. If I had time, probably I could convince certain people, but then, the old adage comes in, "A man convinced against his will is of the same opinion still."
I happened to be reading my bible yesterday and I came to a very important passage of scripture which I think is germane to this discussion. It may seem strange to some that I should read the bible in this connection. May I quote just a part of the thirteenth chapter of Romans:
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
We may not like them. I certainly do not like the Liberal government.
You do not think they are ordained of God.
No, of the people.
In the development of national affairs I suppose some people have to govern Canada.
Even if it happens to be Liberal.
Then the scripture goes on-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I like to hear about the Good Book, but I do not just see how it comes under the present discussion, an item having to do with the Department of Justice. Surely we should come down to earth once in a while and keep to the particular item before us.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that you will not prevent me from reading one or two passages. May I say, speaking on
behalf of the minister, that I realize these things are exacting and quite a responsibility. The scriptures continue:
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same.
The principle is this. Governments attempt to pass laws for the good and the welfare of the people; therefore we should be subject to those laws. I thought, Mr. Chairman, that I had better bring that out because it does not follow that just because the ban is lifted from an organization they can go ahead and do whatever they wish.

Does that apply to
Protestants and Catholics .as well?

It applies to everyone. I belong to a non-denominational church, but I am quite certain that if I went out and preached something that was going to incite a revolution I would not blame the minister if he put me in gaol.
May I add another word? Some of us receive considerable correspondence over these things. It seems that when one brings up a matter in parliament it means additional work for him, because people read it and then he gets a lot of letters. They seem to think the more you do the more you can do. Some of us have received quite a few letters in regard to the authorities not recognizing those who are said to be ordained by Jehovah's Witnesses. I am not going to criticize that; I mention it only in passing, for the purpose of examination. For instance, an ordained minister is exempt from military service, but the mobilization board does not recognize the organization known as Jehovah's Witnesses. I have received a lot of correspondence along that line. I bring it to the attention of the minister so that he may know how the position stands. It can be looked into, but it does not matter to me what decision is made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Does that not arise from a case that was heard in British Columbia, the appeal of which is now. pending?
I could not answer the hon. member's question. I am not informed in that respect.

I do not think we should allow the statements of the hon. member for Macleod to go by without some comment. I think the age-old principle of democracy is freedom of thought, freedom of association and freedom to think and teach on matters
War Appropriation-Justice

of religion as one may feel impelled to think and to teach. I am not a member of any of those unorthodox sects. I happen to belong to one of the very orthodox Protestant communions, but at the same time I feel that the principle which is being challenged of allowing the free distribution of tracts does strike at the very heart of our religious freedom and our conception of democratic institutions.
I was pretty well schooled years ago in the writings of John Milton, and I have never forgotten his "Areopagitica", the plea for the freedom of the press, the plea for the freedom of the right of a man to issue a tract on any particular subject, no matter how distasteful that subject may be to the powers that be. That principle is sound, and is exemplified in the long struggle for the freedom of the press, the freedom of the sect, if you like, to preach and to teach its doctrines which to-day may be unorthodox but which to-morrow may become very orthodox indeed. I always remember the story of two famous bishops. One asked the other how he defined orthodoxy and heterodoxy. He said: "Orthodoxy is my doxy and heterodoxy is the other fellow's doxy." That is precisely what I think we have to bear in mind.

I think that a statement is due from the minister with regard to the whole situation respecting the defence of Canada regulations. In the main those regulations went through the committee in 1940 at a time when conditions were most serious, and the question of survival as a nation and as an empire was paramount in our thoughts. Great Britain has consistently followed the course of removing those encroachments on democratic rights with the gradual dissipation of the danger to the state. I think that the time has come when these regulations as a whole should be reconsidered. In the past we have had committees from year to year on defence of Canada regulations; but unfortunately the recommendations of those committees, composed of outstanding members of the House of Commons, have not been accepted by the minister. When we come to discuss the question of the freedoms we see that freedom of religion is still not completely axistent when we find that the recommendations of the committee have not been implemented. The committee recommended in 1943 that the ban against Jehovah's Witnesses, the International Bible Students' Association and the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society Incorporated should be removed. There can be only one reason for the maintenance of these regulations interfering with religious bodies-that is, the safety of the 
state. I believe there have been some five hundred prosecutions of Jehovah's Witnesses, none of which had to do with subversive activities, the entire offence being that of belonging to an organization banned under the defence of Canada regulations.
What excuse is there for interfering with these people receiving the Holy Bible, regardless of by whom it is published? What is there subversive in their teaching doctrines which the rest of us do not accept, as long as the practice of those doctrines does not interfere with the safety of the state? Why is it that the recommendations of the committee of this house have not been accepted in their entirety by the minister? I ask him to deal specifically with this matter; for if we as members of the House of Commons accept without complaint the principle of interference with the freedom of religion we deny the democracy for which we as a country and empire fight. Britain does not deny these people their rights. The United States does not deny them; Australia does not deny them. Why does this government continue to keep these organizations on the banned list? These are matters that must concern hon. members regardless of party allegiance in this house. I think the time has come when the minister should place the whole story before the house and the country. Why are these organizations banned? Why have they not the right enjoyed by all other church organizations to distribute the literature printed by their own corporations? The ban has been removed, it is said. That is theoretical only, unless the ban is lifted from the organizations which disseminate the literature which these people preach. I do not agree with their principles; I have no appreciation of the stand they take in this war, but I cannot understand how the government may assume to believe in freedom of religion and still deny these people their rights. It may be because of the fact that they do not exercise the franchise, and that in this sense they are not true citizens. In any ease I think the time has come for the minister to tell us the story, to say what are the reasons for the denial to these people of the opportunity to disseminate their own literature; particularly if it is correct, as I believe it is, that not one case of subversive activities has been brought home to these people.

I would point out that the head office of the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society is in London, England. Their publications are not banned there; why should they be banned in Canada? I should like an answer from the minister.

speechtext: The hon. member for Cartier has the floor.

Surely we are
entitled to an answer.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am asking this committee to vote the sum of $30,000 for the expenses of the advisory committees which deal with the cases of the internees; that is all I am asking.
Mr. HANSON (York-SunbupO : Well, now, the minister won't get away with that.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The minister is not trying to get away with anything. If it pleases this committee to travel over the field of war activities since the beginning of the war, that is its privilege until the chairman sees fit to intervene, but so' far as I am concerned I am going to try to stick to the matters with which I have to deal.

The minister knows as well as I know and as every other member of this committee knows that this is the only item in this war appropriation resolution under which we can discuss the defence of Canada regulations. The fact that this item is for payment of the expenses of the advisory committees does not alter the situation at all; we have a right to know the facts; and the minister ought not, I say with respect-because I have great respect for him- to take the attitude he is taking to-day, that he wishes to deal only with the question of the voting of the money to pay these advisory committees. There are people in this country who want to know why these regulations have not been relaxed, in view of the fact, as stated by my colleague from Lake Centre, that the danger to the state is no longer as threatening as it was. Why should not these regulations be relaxed? I quite appreciate that in the early days of the war, when people were on edge, when there was an imminent threat of invasion, when people had a different attitude towards this sort of thing, there should be strict rules against anything that might be subversive. That day is past. I had the pleasure of sitting in at a meeting of the committee on the defence of Canada regulations when Sir Norman Birkett appeared before the committee and gave a wonderful exposition of the attitude of the British people and of the committees over there in relation to all classes in the community, including communists, if you will. Why should Canada's attitude be so strict as compared with the
attitude of Britain and other countries I could mention?
While I am on my feet I should like to
know if it is open to us as members of this committee to ask about individual cases of internees who have been released, and the reasons therefor. I will make just one allusion; I refer to the case of Mr. Camillien Houde, who is interned in a community not very far from where I live. The story in that part of the country is that he was offered his release under certain conditions, with which he refused to comply. So far as I am concerned that is hearsay; I do not make any allegations or charges. It may not be open to give me the facts; I realize that they have to be treated with circumspection and that the reports of these advisory committees should be and are in the main secret. We are not very far apart on that principle, but statements are going round the country that the government is trying through these committees to drive bargains with certain gentlemen, and the country ought to know if that is true. If not, it should be denied and the position set at rest. But the minister must tell us what changes have been made in the defence of Canada regulations, what are contemplated to be made, and what is the policy of the government. Do they intend to relax these regulations, and in what direction?

Mr. Chairman, the hon member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has just referred to the detention of Mr. Camillien Houde, former mayor of Montreal and member of the Quebec legislature. Would the minister say whether he is detained under the defence of Canada regulations or under the mobilization act regulations and for what offence? Is the infraction related to one or the other of the above mentioned regulations? I do not intend to defend Mr. Camillien Houde in particular, but a principle is involved. Being a British subject, he is entitled to fair play as any other British citizen. If he has committed an offence, let him be tried and, if found guilty, condemned to a penalty; but he is entitled to know whether he is to be held indefinitely, without being informed of the penalty he has incurred. I believe the public is entitled to be informed by the minister of the offence committed, the penalty incurred and of whether or not his detention is for an indefinite period.
