speechtext:
The hon. member for Cartier has the floor.
War Appropriation-Justice

No; I want an answer. I have asked questions of the Minister of Justice, and I am entitled to an answer.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: A great many questions have been asked, some of which concern the defence of Canada regulations. Others have been dealt with by the Minister of National Defence. It is difficult to determine at what point members in the committee wish an answer that would be pertinent to the item before the committee, and at what point they merely desire to air some grievances with which I am not concerned. If it is proper for me to do so, I shall endeavour to deal with some of the matters relating to the defence of Canada regulations. However I should like to hear what other members of the committee wish to say on that point.
Perhaps I can take up the questions in reverse order to that in which they have been asked. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie wants to know under what regulations Mr. Camillien Houde was interned. My answer is that he was interned under regulation 21 of the defence of Canada regulations. The hon. member wants to know what infraction had been committed. Internment is not punishment for having committed an infraction. Internment is an order made by the Minister of Justice, in the exercise of the confidence the house has placed in him, to restrict the liberties of an individual, if he is satisfied it is necessary so to do, with a view to preventing that individual from acting in any manner prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state. The order against Mr. Camillien Houde was made because Mr. Houde was acting in a manner which the Minister of Justice then felt constituted something 'prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state. Mr. Camillien Houde was recommending to the public, in a part of this country in which he felt he had support, that there be refusal to comply with national registration regulations. It was felt that that ' was prejudicial to the safety of the state, and for that reason his internment was ordered. For a long time he was not disposed to ask to have his case reviewed by an advisory board under the authority of the defence of Canada regulations. However, on May 10, 1943, he requested that he be given a hearing. This letter was received by the Department of Justice on May 15, and arrangements were made immediately to have an advisory committee meet and proceed to Fredericton, not only because Mr. Houde had asked to be heard, but because at that time there was a number of applications sufficient to warrant the holding of sittings of the advisory board at that point.
[The Chairman.]
Mr. Houde came before the board at Fredericton in the course of these hearings on May 28 and 29, 1943. As a result of questions put by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains, it has already been communicated to the house that in the course of its inquiry the committee had to know what Mr. Houde's present dispositions were, and asked him if he would be prepared to sign the usual form of undertaking signed by a great many of those released from internment. This is an undertaking to abide by the laws of Canada, and to do nothing to interfere with the prosecution of Canada's war effort. He asked that a copy of the usual conditions be delivered to him, and said that he would answer the next day. Next day he informed the committee that he was not disposed to sign anything. Thereupon a report was made to the Minister of Justice recommending that his detention be continued.

Is it a condition precedent to release that an internee shall sign this undertaking?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is not a condition precedent to release. Members of the advisory committee try to make such investigation as will convince them as to whether if he were released the internee would be apt to act in a manner prejudicial to the safety of the state. On their own motion, having received no suggestion whatsoever, from the Department of Justice, they have adopted the procedure of saying to the individual, "Are you sincere in your statement that you are disposed to do everything within your power, with the exception of enrolling in the army, or taking part in the activities of the active army, to further Canada's war effort?" This is asked of a person of enemy origin. A great many of them have declared that they were so disposed. Then they are asked, "Are you so seriously disposed to that end that you would be willing to sign an undertaking to that effect?" A great many have said that they were. And it is after having agreed to sign such an undertaking that in many cases recommendations for release are made, the advisory board holding the view that the individual would not be a danger to the safety of the state.

In practice it is a condition precedent-if not in theory.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not go so far as to say that in practice it is a condition precedent.

Has any man been released who did not sign?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

War Appropriation-Justice

Of course that is the answer.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Yes, there were
releases before this practice was adopted. But there has been no recommendation to release a person who refused, or who said he was not disposed to sign such an undertaking. If a person were not disposed to sign an undertaking of the kind, such decision evidently influenced the judgment of members of the advisory board, and there was no recommendation for release.

It is to show his bona fides.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, to show his bona fides. Then, in November, 1943, Mr. Houde wrote a letter to Joseph Jean, parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice, in which he indicated he would be prepared to sign an undertaking. This letter was communicated to me. I told Mr. Jean that was not the regular way of communicating with the Department of Justice; that if Mr. Houde had any communication to address to that department he should address it to the department and not to a member of parliament who happens to be parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice.
I assume that he was given that kind of answer. On December 11 Mr. Houde wrote the deputy minister of the department saying that he was prepared to sign the kind of undertaking that had been submitted to him when the advisory committee had considered his case in May. A reply was made to him that arrangements were being made to have his file placed before the. advisory committee which was to visit Fredericton some time in January, and that he might make another appearance before them and allow them to report on the probability or otherwise of his behaving in such manner as would not interfere with the prosecution of our war effort.
Under date of January 10 Mr. Houde wrote the deputy minister of justice that he did not want any further hearing, and a copy of that letter was tabled in this house. Subsequently an hon. member of this house came to see me and said that Mr. Houde, as was stated in this letter of which a copy was tabled, had expressed the view that he had been interned by order in council and that he was going to come out through the big door and there would have to be an order in council passed to let him out. I explained to the hon. member that he 'was quite mistaken; that Mr. Houde had been treated like any other Canadian or resident of Canada under the defence of Canada regulations; that an order had been made by the Minister of Justice, and if he wanted that order reconsidered-it had been reconsidered once-it could be reconsidered again. He was told that there could not be any special procedure for Mr. Houde, and that unless and until a recommendation was made for his release in conformity with the regulations he would unfortunately have to stay in internment.
I am sorry to take up so much time with this, but apparently there has been a great deal of public interest focussed on this matter and it p'erhaps justifies the time I am taking. On March 19, 1944, Mr. Houde wrote as follows:
Mr. Liguori Lacombe, the federal member for the constituency of Laval-Two Mountains, has informed me in a letter dated the 7 th instant, of an interview that he has had with the Minister of Justice concerning the early termination of my detention.
Following that interview he advises me to apply for a revision of my case, the reason offered being that I was misinformed when in my last letter to your department I stated that I had been interned by an order in council.
Considering the untiring efforts of Mr. Laeom.be on my behalf I readily comply with what, under the circumstances, seems to be a reasonable request, and I hereby apply for such a revision.
Would you kindly inform me, at your earliest convenience, of any decision in this matter, and oblige.
Thereupon the deputy minister replied to Mr. Houde as follows:
I have discussed with the minister your letter of March 19.
It is quite true that Mr. Liguori Lacombe did go to see the minister and his object in doing so was probably to endeavour to obtain an early termination of your detention. I do not know what information Mr. Lacombe wrote you, but the minister tells me that his only statement to Mr. Lacombe was that you were entirely mistaken in your previous letter in stating that you had been interned by an order in council; he pointed out that you had in fact been interned by virtue of an order made by the Minister of Justice under the defence of Canada regulations and that if and when you were released it would have to be in conformity with the procedure set up by these regulations.
In your last letter you "apply for a revision of my ease." Am I to take it from this letter that it is an application for a hearing before an advisory committee operating under the regulations? It is intended to have such a committee sit again at Fredericton during the month of May, and if it is your desire to have a hearing before that committee please let me know so that definite consideration can be given to such an application.
On April 17 Mr. Houde replied to the deputy minister as follows:
In answer to your letter of the 28th last I hereby apply for a revision of my case under the defence of Canada regulations before an advisory committee operating under said regulations.
For your information I beg to state that Mr. Lacombe. in his letter to me, has simply suggested that I should ask for a revision of my case, and I thought it best in my letter to you to use the same phraseology.
War Appropriation-Justice

Whatever his reason' may have been, on April 17 he asked that his case be reviewed by an advisory committee under the defence of Canada regulations. A committee set up under the defence of Canada regulations is to proceed shortly to Fredericton to consider a number of applications for rehearing; Mr. Houde's file is being handed to that committee, and he will be accorded a rehearing at that time.

That is
Mr. Houde up to date.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That brings the matter up to date. This was not punishment for an offence; it was something done to prevent him from acting in a manner which it was felt would be prejudicial to the interests of the state. Since he has persisted in that attitude up to the present time, no committee has taken upon itself to recommend that he be released.

I must say that I am far from satisfied with the explanation given by the minister. We have laws in this country; we have the criminal code and we have other regulations. If a man does not comply with the law, he is prosecuted; if he is convicted there is a penalty, but he knows wha't to expect. All I am asking for Camillien Houde is that he be given the same treatment as is given to any other British subject, nothing more.
At the beginning of his explanation the minister said that Mr. Houde had been interned because he had not complied with the regulations of the mobilization act. Then at the end of his explanation I was under the impression that he said Mr. Houde had not complied with the defence of Canada regulations. In either case there is a penalty, and he should know to what penalty he is exposed. When a man refuses to comply with the regulations of the mobilization act he is prosecuted before a criminal court. He may be found guilty, but he should not be asked to sign a document 3uch as Mr. Houde was asked to sign. I think it is unfair to say that as long as Mr. Camillien Houde refuses to register in accordance with the mobilization act he will not be released unless he signs some kind of document. The defence of Canada regulations state:
(Translation):
63. (1) Every person who contravenes or fails to comply with any of these regulations, or any order, rule, by-law, or direction, made or given under any of these regulations, shall be guilty of an offence against that regulation.
(2) Where no specific penalty is provided, such person shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars,
[ Mr. St. Laurent.l
or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding twelve months, or to both fine and imprisonment; but such person may, at the election of the Attorney General of Canada or of the province, be prosecuted upon indictment, and if convicted shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or to both fine and imprisonment.
It states distinctly that there is no other penalty. When a man has committed an infraction of the defence of Canada regulations he is prosecuted in the courts and condemned to a fine or imprisonment. In the case of Camillien Houde, he has been there for the last four years. He has not committed any other offence than have people who have been brought before the courts of this country in every province because they have refused to comply with the regulations under the mobilization act, that is, refused to register. That is the infraction which he has committed, and although he has been in detention for four years he is still detained and is to be kept in detention until he signs an agreement according to the pleasure of the Minister of Justice. In my opinion this is entirely unfair. I believe the public is very much interested, because Mr. Houde has not received the treatment which is guaranteed to any ordinary citizen of this country.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sorry that the hon. member is not satisfied with the explanation, but the fact is that Mr. Houde was not interned because he refused to comply with the national registration regulations; he was interned because he was taking an attitude to encourage people over whom he had influence not to comply with the regulations.

He signed a written statement.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He signed a statement to that effect, advising them not to comply with that provision of the law; and so long as this country is at war, and so long as I have the responsibility of administering the defence of Canada regulations, I shall not feel it possible to consider that such conduct is not prejudicial to the safety of the state.
Now, to deal with other matters which were raised in connection with the defence of Canada regulations.

I understand that Tim Buck has been released. Was he obliged to sign any statement before he was released?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No one was obliged to sign any statement; but before Mr. Tim Buck was released he did declare that it was his intention to comply with the laws and regulations of Canada and to contribute to

War Appropriation-Justice
the best of his ability to Canada's war effort. As an evidence of his good faith he signed a statement to that effect; it was after he had stated his willingness to sign such a statement that an advisory committee recommended to the Department of Justice that he be released, and it was only after he had done so that he was released.

I understand that Mr. Houde has written a letter to Mr. Jean to that effect.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Jean is not an advisory committee under the defence of Canada regulations, and Mr. Camillien Houde is not going to be treated any differently from any other resident of Canada who was interned under the defence of Canada regulations.

But Tim Buck did not send his statement to an advisory committee.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Tim Buck was heard before an advisory committee; it was before an advisory committee that he made that statement, and it was as agreed before an advisory committee that he signed his undertaking in writing. Thereafter the recommendation of the committee was made to the Department of Justice and an order for release was signed, as recommended.

Was Mr. Tim Buck interned?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

No.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He surrendered for internment and was interned, and immediately afterwards went before an advisory committee and succeeded in convincing the committee that it should report that his being at large at this time would not endanger the safety of the state.

What was the duration of the internment?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Less than a month.

How long did he hide from the police?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: From some time in June, 1940, until some time in, I think it was August, 1942. I can get the exact date if the hon. member is interested.
A further question was with respect to the possible danger to the safety of the state in any publications emanating from associations connected with Jehovah's Witnesses, with respect to which the ban was not lifted at the time that it was withdrawn from the organization itself. The reason for that is that, in my view of the defence of Canada regulationsand I am the one who has to take the responsibility of their application-it is contrary to the policy of the state, contrary to the public interest, that the doctrine of not being bound by man-made laws should be taught. There were two points principally upon which publications emanating from this organization were held to be contrary to the public interest and the safety of the state. One, which is very similar to the attitude for which Mr. Houde is still interned, was that man-made laws need not be complied with. The second point was the propaganda to the effect that one could be an ordained minister of Jehovah's Witnesses by making an individual compact with the Almighty, that by doing so one became an ordained minister and not subject to the mobilization regulations. That is something which I look upon as contrary to the policy which this state has to maintain in war time. It cannot be left to the individual to say, "I have by consecrating myself to the Almighty made myself an ordained minister, and thus brought myself within the exceptions provided by the mobilization regulations." Some of the publications which emanate from these associated organizations-I am sorry I cannot say whether the head office is in London, England, but I was under the impression that it is a United States organization- are unnecessary to any of the persons who in good faith assume to satisfy their conscience by the form of worship of Jehovah's Witnesses, to enable them to worship the Almighty in the manner in which they see fit, and they contain material the propagation of which I look upon as contrary to the policy this state has to follow under war conditions.
Freedom to think and to teach is fully recognized, provided what is taught is not in itself subversive. But it is subversive of our order at the present time to teach that individuals are not bound by any man-made laws. It is subversive to teach that any young man can by this private pact bring himself outside the regulations which are required for the purpose of military service in this country.

By the minister's definition it is subversive to state that one is not bound by man-made laws. Does he set up a different definition of what is subversive from that accepted by Great Britain, the United States and Australia? If so, why?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Perhaps I should not have used the word "subversive". I should have said, contrary to the policy which this state must enforce in war time.
Why are we different from these other countries?

It is subversive.
War Appropriation-Justice

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know what the situation is in those countries. The hon. member said there had been a great many prosecutions of persons who were Jehovah's Witnesses. I know there were a large number of prosecutions for border offences of persons who- happened to be Jehovah's Witnesses, because, being Jehovah's Witnesses, they felt they could disregard man-made laws and go into the United States and attend some sort of religious meeting over there, and they were prosecuted for violation of border-crossing regulations. That is something which, in my view, manifests no interference whatsoever with liberty of conscience. There may be a great many people in this country or elsewhere who would feel it would satisfy their conscience to make certain pilgrimages to places which are now not accessible and which would require them to go out of this country, but they would not be allowed to proceed out of this country unless they complied with the regulations set up in that behalf.

But there were prosecutions for delivering tracts in the county of Beauee-a most disgraceful thing.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, I know. But there are 11,500,000 Canadians; they are not all in the Department of Justice and I cannot be held responsible for errors that may be committed elsewhere. This matter was raised at the last session and I stated frankly that I had seen these tracts and they were extracts from the French edition of the Bible published over the name of l'abbe Crampon, which is a well recognized edition that is used by Roman Catholics of the French language, and there did not seem to be anything else but that. It certainly was a mistake to prosecute anyone for distributing copies of pages of the bible if there was nothing more. There have been overzealous officials in all administrations, and that was certainly something that should not have been done. I may say that it was one of the reasons which made it appear necessary to me to go farther than had first been done in respect of Jehovah's Witnesses.
My first recommendation had been a modification which would allow them to exercise their religion in any way they saw fit; but the fact that they remained banned was something which possibly encouraged overzealous prosecutions that were taking place in different parts of Canada, and I felt, that because of that it would be better to remove the ban in the defence of Canada regulations, and that, if prosecutions had to be instituted, to institute them under the criminal code. It was for that reason that it was done. But, as one hon. member has pointed out in this

house, it has created among some the impression that now anything which a person who calls himself a Jehovah's Witness does is legal, simply because the ban has been lifted. That of course is not seriously contended anywhere, and it is an impression which is no more justified than was the impression that because Jehovah's Witnesses distributed extracts from the bible they were doing something illegal.
The other matters dealt with the treatment of Jehovah's Witnesses in military camps. I am sure every hon. member knows that the Minister of National Defence will not tolerate anything of that kind in the camps under his jurisdiction, and whenever anything of the kind is brought to his attention it is carefully inquired into and if what is stated on hearsay evidence is to be disproved it will be disproved. If it turns out that there is some justification in fact for any part of it, the parties responsible will be severely dealt with.
Other matters that were raised had to do with the releasing from internment of Lorimer, Farr and Schneider. John Lorimer and Joseph Farr had been interned in June, 1940, under regulation 21 of the defence of Canada regulations as partisans of the National Unity party of which Adrien Arcand, who is still interned, was the recognized leader. Both Lorimer and Farr had had some connection with it. Lorimer was alleged to have held office -as assistant treasurer and Farr was an officer of the organization. He was an organizer. Lorimer had a hearing before Mr. Justice Fortier in 1940; after that hearing it was recommended that his detention should be continued, and it was continued. He had a further hearing before a three-man committee in July, 1942. That committee, after considering all the angles of the case, recommended that he be released. He had succeeded in convincing the committee that he had had little to do with the organization, that he had manifested, even while interned, that he was in full sympathy with the war effort of this country and of the allies, and that he was ready to do everything in his -power to further the war effort to the united nations. He had stated that he was quite willing to put his signature to a declaration to that effect, and as a matter of fact he did. They recommended that he be released and he was released on September 1, 1942. One of the conditions of his release was that he should report monthly to the R.C.M.P. and he has been doing so. They have kept in touch with him since; he seems to be the sort of person who found it was at least uncomfortable to have been in the limelight; he wanted to drop back into his original obscurity and he has dropped back.

War Appropriation-Justice

He wanted to go back into private life, did he?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Apart from his
monthly reports, nothing further has been heard about him since. Farr bad been interned at the same time. He had a hearing in December, 1940, before Mr. Justice Fortier; continuation of his detention had been recommended and it was continued.
In August, 1942, he was again heard before the same committee that heard Lorimer. At that time he was not able to convince the committee that he was then in a frame of mind where his activities would no longer be a threat to the safety of the state. They recommended that his detention be continued. Shortly afterwards he got into very serious difficulties with the nazi elements in the camp and was pretty severely beaten up on several occasions because of the attitude he was expressing in the camp owing to his consideration for the cause of the allied nations. He had a new hearing in July, 1943, and in October, 1943. After the committee obtained further information about him and became convinced-at least so they certified-that his being at liberty at that time would in no way endanger the safety of the state, he also having signed an undertaking to that effect, and having been informed that he would be required to report monthly to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, he was released. He also has been reporting monthly since that time, and other than from his report we have heard nothing about him. He has dropped back into private life. The information we have is that he will never again be in with the kind of party that he belonged to at the time he was interned. One of those releases was made in September, 1942, and the other one in October, 1943.
Some weeks ago I think the PM newspaper heard that these men had been released and compared what had taken place here with the stir that had been occasioned by the release of one Mr. Mosley in the United Kingdom. As a matter of fact these men had dropped back into private life here and had behaved themselves, and no one connected with either the police or in any other connection had found that any inconvenience to the safety or well-being of the state had resulted. Unless and until something takes place which would convince me that it would be my duty, for the protection of the state, to re-intern them, I would certainly not do so. I have received a large number of communications from various parts of the country requesting that these men be re-intemed and that an undertaking be given that they will
remain interned for the duration of the war. I replied that it seemed to me to be a most undemocratic suggestion to make; that no one could or should be detained unless there was such evidence as convinced the Minister of Justice that it was necessary to do so to prevent them from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety or to the safety of the state. And to suggest, because one was called Lorimer and the other Farr, that they be re-interned and that an undertaking be given that they would remain interned for the duration was not a procedure that I could contemplate as a proper one.
I may say right here that no one in the Department of Justice makes any suggestion whatsoever to the members of these committees, each one of which is presided over by a judge, as to what attitude they shall take. There has been no change of policy; there has been a change in conditions. In June, 1940, when it became apparent that there had been fifth-column activity to the extent which was revealed by the tactics in the countries which were overrun, all hon. members remember that there was considerable nervousness in this country and that it was easy for any one who happened to be in the office of the Minister of Justice at that time to come to the conclusion that it might be necessary to order such-and-so for the safety of the state. Large numbers of residents of Canada of German and Italian origin were then interned and since that time a great many of them have been having their individual cases carefully considered and have been released. I do not think a mistake was made in interning them. I think one has to look back to the conditions which existed at that time, and at that time the condition was so urgent that there was no opportunity to examine in advance with the care that has been given to the individual cases since. The Minister of Justice could not afford to take any risks at that time. Fortunately, since that time the situation has considerably improved and something which made the change in the attitude of the Department of Justice to these questions is the entry of the United States into the war. The cooperation which has existed since that time between the R.C.M.P. and the F.B.I. is such that as to the facts and the probabilities a different impression has been created.

Would the minister permit a question before he passes on to the next subject? Will he tell us how many residents of Canada are still interned and how many were released during the last year?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is the figure I was looking for. There are still over 300 persons other than persons of Japanese origin.
War Appropriation-Justice
COMMONS [DOT]
I segregated them because the Japanese situation is one that arose at a later date and has been dealt with in a separate compartment.

Does that include all
persons of enemy nationality other than Japanese?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are about 160 British subjects who are still interned; that is, British subjects by birth or by naturalization.

Is it broken down as to
racial origin?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	There are held as
enemy aliens under regulation 25, 141 of German origin. There are held under regulation 21, as residents of Canada, being British subjects by birth and naturalization, but of German racial origin, 120; of Italian racial origin, 2; of Italian origin, naturalized, 4; others, principally because of their connections with this unity national party, 32.

No Austrians or Hungarians?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	They have been
grouped with the Germans.
There was one other case about which explanations were asked; that was the case of A. N. Schneider. As has been stated, this man was first detained in September, 1939, and released in December of the same year. His release, I understand, was the cause of many protests to the department at that time. In June, 1940, when these orders for detention were being issued against a large number of residents of Canada of German and Italian origin, he was again included and interned. He had a hearing before an advisory committee in September, 1942, and the committee recommended continued detention. He was heard again in February, 1944, at which time he was able to convince the advisory committee, which is one that has been functioning since I came into the department, which has had a great deal of experience, to which no suggestion has ever been made by the government, and with respect to which I would resent any suggestion being made by the Department of Justice-

Is the minister free to give the personnel of that committee?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. The chairman is His Honour Judge M. A. Miller; the members of the committee are Mr. Robert Taschereau, K.C., former chairman of the workmen's compensation board of the province of Quebec, and Mr. W. M. Dickson, former deputy minister of labour. That committee made a report in

February, 1944, recommending that this man be released, and the file and recommendation came before me. Of course in many of these cases it would be convenient to be able to give the facts; but it has been felt that it would be improper to give them in one case and refuse to give them in another. For that reason when the question was put by the hon. member for Saskatoon City it was felt that all we could say were the facts which were known. Certainly it does not make a man a safe person to have at large in the country because he happens to have two nephews in the armed forces overseas or because he happens to have a son who has not reached the age when he can enter the army but who has entered the reserve cadet group in his locality. But those facts were notorious; and together with other facts which were brought out in the evidence before the committee they convinced the committee that this man was not now, if ever he had been, a nazi sympathizer, and that it would not be a danger to the security of the state to allow him to be released. Here again, as evidence of good faith, he declared his willingness to sign this undertaking and was released in the ordinary course.

Was he interned because he was a nazi sympathizer?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He was interned at the time all the Germans were being picked up, being interned first in September, 1939, on reports that had been received from the locality in which he lived. Those reports were investigated and found to be not sufficient, so that he was released in December, 1939. Then when the general order was being made, in June, 1940, to pick up all the nazi or fascist sympathizers throughout the country, he was included in the list.

If the minister will permit me, while it is hard to know what facts are acceptable and what are not, as the minister knows this Doctor Schneider was alleged to have been very much interested in the election campaign of 1940. It was difficult for the public to understand why he should be picked up and released just before the election; then picked up again after the election was over. When all the parts of this apparent puzzle are put together, of course the public are led to believe what has been stated often in the house and what perhaps will remain in the public mind for a long time.
He will have a chance to do a better election job this summer.

That explanation
does not quite agree with the explanation given

War Appropriation-Justice
by the former Minister of Justice who, speaking in this house on June 13, 1940, at page 745 of Hansard, said:
In one case, which was in Saskatchewan, the man was released under special circumstances in December.
I point out that the minister now says he was released as the result of a finding in his favour.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not in December. At that time the system of advisory boards had not been set up. I said after an investigation, but not after a hearing.

The former minister went on:
I was told by my good friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that this man took part in the election which followed. Well, if he did, it did not serve him very well, because I have since ordered his reinternment and he is still in the camp. I [DOT]have no qualms of conscience as to that case at all. I cannot give to the house the circumstances, but at least one condition of his release was not lived up to, and this circumstance permitted me to order his reinternment.
Then the minister went on to describe a case in the province of Manitoba, of a man with the same surname; he said he had ordered that man's reintemment but felt that it was unfair to have done so, though he had to do it in the circumstances. I point out, Mr. Chairman, that between January 25, 1940, which was about the time the writs for the election were issued, and March 26, 1940, which was the date of the election, fifty per cent of those interned in Saskatchewan were released. That is why there was a feeling that considerations other than the safety of the state had entered into the equation. At that time the minister assured the house that this was not the case.
I should like to say one thing for the minister. While extraordinary powers are given under the defence of Canada regulations in the matter of internment, since becoming minister the hon. gentleman has seen to it that no one has been kept interned after his release has been recommended by an advisory committee, thereby removing the complaint so often heard that unless the minister acted in that way, too great powers were thereby exercised by him.
Now, with respect to internees who are British subjects by naturalization, men who have endeavoured by subversive activities to undermine this country in a time of war, and whose activities have been designed to assist the enemy, has the minister given consideration to recommending a change in the law whereby their naturalization certificates will be cancelled, and whereby when the war is
over such people will be returned to those countries they have actively endeavoured to support during this time of war?
It seems difficult to understand why people who came to this country and accepted the honour of citizenship, but who have endeavoured to undermine the state, should after their discharge be permitted to resume their activities as citizens of this country and receive the protection and the honour that British citizenship carries with it. Some amendment or some change in the law should be effected whereby such people would be sent back to the countries the causes of which they have espoused during this period of war. That is the only way in which that vast number of citizens who have come from alien enemy countries but who have remained true and loyal to Canada will receive proper and fair consideration for what they have done during the period of war. They have supported Canada, and they have the right to ask that those who have acted in a treasonable manner shall receive something more than internment.
I think of a man in Saskatchewan living near the town of Gull Lake, who served in the German army before coming to Canada. His son, while a sergeant-pilot in this war, earned the D.F.M., was commissioned, and is to-day a flying officer. To such men, all honour; but with respect to those others who have accepted citizenship in Canada, and at the same time have endeavoured to undermine this country in a time of war, no consideration, political or otherwise, should be permitted to intervene with their being sent back to those countries they have endeavoured to support, while at the same time accepting the protection of British citizenship.

I have listened with interest to the explanations given by the minister, particularly that concerning the Schneider case. As the evidence will appear, Mr. Schneider was released as the result of a recommendation by an advisory committee. I am not for a moment questioning the integrity of advisory committees, but I urge that they should be careful not to relax their vigilance in respect of people who have been placed in internment camps as a result of investigations instituted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
It is true that in June, 1940, this country was considerably aroused and concerned about these matters, and that possibly the vigilance was somewhat greater than necessary. Nevertheless the Schneider case was investigated on September 22, 1942, which is some considerable time later. I presume careful consideration was given to it at that time, and that all evidence was before the committee. The result of the investigation was a recommendation that detention be continued. I
War Appropriation-Justice

suggest to the minister, and through him to the advisory committee, that the fact the war is looking somewhat better for us should not cause us to relax our vigilance in respect of these suspects.
These signed documents, under which these people promise to be good boys-I think we may put it in that way-do not amount to much. Hitler made promises and did not keep them; and there are lots of other people who are prepared to make promises, but who are not ready to keep them.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Perhaps it is more significant when one refuses to sign.

I doubt that; I should be inclined to think the opposite.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not always. However, the matter raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre is and has been for some time receiving careful attention. I believe we shall have at our disposal the results of carefully made and independent investigations into the histories of each of these persons. We shall be in a position to make such use of those histories as may be proper under the conditions of any peace treaty which will be established.
At this time I do not think it would be wise to go farther. We are not going to be unfair to anyone, whatever his origin. That has been the attitude of the government, particularly the departments of External Affairs and National Defence. They have insisted upon the maintenance of that attitude. It is one which I believe should be maintained, because we do not want any other country, some citizens of which may be in Canada, to be unfair to Canadian citizens who are held in such countries as prisoners of war or otherwise. We shall have made investigations which will enable us to have the facts, and we shall be in a position to take the action which may be indicated by those facts.

My understanding is that when a person who holds a naturalization certificate as a British subject is found guilty of subversive activities, such certificate 's not automatically cancelled?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; but that is a matter which is receiving attention. An interdepartmental committee which acts in an advisory capacity has been set up. It will be supplied with all the information, and will have the facts in respect of each case in which action might be taken. I am quite sure the hon. member is not suggesting that a person who is a naturalized British subject and who has been interned should be considered as having against him a conviction for subversive activity. The possibility of subversive

activity is all that is required to bring the Minister of Justice to the conclusion that for the safety of the state it is necessary to order internment.
The minister does not attempt to make a conviction. That would mean that the benefit of the doubt would be in favour of the person whose case might be under consideration. Under the defence of Canada regulations it has been and is the practice of placing the benefit of the doubt in favour of the state. If there is any doubt as to a man's being dangerous, such doubt must be resolved in favour of the state. It may be unfortunate in some cases that persons whose intentions and motives and conduct may be innocent should suffer. Nevertheless the rule I have indicated is the one we find it necessary to apply in respect of the administration of these regulations. When it comes to imposing penal sanction-and none could be greater than the cancellation of one's naturalization certificate -we would require the kind of evidence which would justify a conviction.

Upon review of a number of cases it has been found that original internment was carried out for no reason other than the one that the internees were of enemy extraction, but were also British citizens. I know of many cases of that kind. Upon review it has been found that these internees have not been dangerous. Is there any move to give them redress for their internment?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, there is not. The regulations were administered for the safety of the state and it has not been felt that any consideration should be given to such cases. Should a case arise where there has been a glaring mistake owing to negligence, that would be another matter.

At the time I had reference to there was a certain amount of hysteria in the country. This was quite natural, as the minister has explained, owing to the possibilities of subversive activities, but perhaps numbers of persons were interned who should not have been. I have in mind a man who was a really good citizen, a builder who employed many men. I do not know why he was taken up, but he was sent to an internment camp and kept there for quite a while before he was released. Three of his sons were in the army and the fact that he was interned had broken up his entire family. His wife's health has failed and I was just wondering if in a review of any such case there would be any redress.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I will just make a note of that.

Kettle Valley Railway

My hon. friend says that he knows of a case where an error was made. I have some knowledge of the operations of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Department of Justice in the earlier, stressful days to which my hon. friend refers. There have been remarkably few cases of error in internment, but the situation has changed and releases have been made after careful and full investigation. However, I should not like my hon. friend-and perhaps he did not intend to-to cast any reflection upon the magnificent record of our secret service as carried out by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in times of great stress, at a time when the mother country had her back to the wall and when there was a growing rumble of subversive activities. In that connection I should like to pay a tribute to the fine work and the few mistakes made in connection with the entire administration of internment operations in this country.

I have nothing to say against the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. On the contrary I shall have some fine words to say about them when that matter is before us. That does not come under this item. I was assuming from what the minister said that a large number of internments had been made at a time when there was considerable hysteria, but that to-day only a small number comparatively speaking are still interned. I have known the man to whom I referred for many years, although I cannot say whether he committed any subversive action. He was of Italian origin and his family were highly respected. At that time many Italians were loaded in vans and taken away, and I was wondering if there might not be some redress made in cases like this. Simply because a man is of a certain nationality should not warrant his being unnecessarily, one might say abused, although that is not the right word- perhaps suppressed would be better. We shall never build up a country out of different races, as have our neighbours to the south, unless we have a more human understanding of those different races. This man had a family of seven, all born here in Canada, and several are now in the armed forces. This may be only one case-it is not for me -to say-but I merely asked the minister if such cases were being considered. He has said that it will be looked into. I have a very high regard for the Minister of Justice because I have always found him very fair in giving his answers.

I understand that under the regulations a man who is interned cannot run for an election. If Camillien Houde is successful in his application, would he then be in position to stand for election to the various legislative bodies in the country?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have been warned several times that it is improper for the Minister of Justice to attempt to give a legal opinion from his seat in the house. I shall refer my hon. friend to the regulation and ask him to draw his own conclusion. It is No. 65, which reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained in any statute or other law, no person who has been detained or interned under the provisions of these regulations, and while so detained or interned, or who has been convicted of any offence against regulation 39C of these regulations, shall be eligible as a candidate for any public office at any municipal, provincial or dominion election, or otherwise.
That regulation creates an obstacle while a man is interned. As to whether or not there would be an obstacle resulting from internment after his release would, I suggest, depend upon the terms of the provincial or municipal statute that governed the eligibility of candidates for election.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Yale) moved the second reading of bill No. 88, respecting the Kettle Valley Railway Company.
He said: I move the second reading of this bill in the hope that it will be sent to the standing committee on railways. Forty years ago the company had power to construct this branch line, but did not do so, or did so only in part, and the desire now is to continue that construction for another ten miles down to a place called Osoyoos, a little north of the United States boundary, where there is a considerable volume of produce to be picked up. The branch line at present stops thirty miles or so south of Penticton, and if the railway is not continued for the other ten miles, the produce from that area, which is continually increasing, will have to be carried by truck on the highway, at the expense of both gas and rubber. The railway company is of opinion that now is the time to continue-the construction to this other point of collection.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
Fundy Air Lines

Mr. V. J. POTTIER (Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare) moved the second reading of bill No. 89, to incorporate Fundy Air Lines.
He said: In moving the second reading of this bill, I would call to the attention of the house that order in council P.C. 2200, passed on May 18, 1943, provided that "during the present war or until otherwise ordered by the governor in council no further letters of patent under part 1 of the Companies Act as amended be granted incorporating a company having as a principal object or purpose the operation of aircraft in Canada or between Canada and other countries." That same order in section 2 provides that "applicants should be advised, if they desire to incorporate companies with this particular object or purpose, to apply for incorporation by act of parliament."
I wish to emphasize that the proposed bill does not involve the granting of any specific licence or route to actually engage in air operations between specified points or otherwise operate aircraft. The petition is purely and simply for the incorporation of a company which cannot now be incorporated by letters of patent or charter.
Before Fundy Air Lines, if incorporated, can actually operate, it will be necessary to secure a licence from the Department of Transport which, speaking generally, would warrant the airworthiness of their aircraft, and also to secure a licence from the board of transport commissioners to fly between such points and places as may from time to time be named by order in council. The board of transport commissioners, as the law stands at present, have the sole right to grant licences but only between such points and places as have been named by order in council. It is understood that a number of applications are at present pending before the board of transport commissioners but cannot be dealt with until appropriate orders in council have been passed. The powers asked for in the proposed bill are those usually required to set up company machinery with authority to carry on air line services.

I do not rise for the purpose of opposing the second reading of this bill. What I understand the applicants are asking for is a charter which has been denied them by the order in council referred to by the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill; that is to say, an amendment made under the War Measures Act to the first part of the Companies Act; an amendment made while parliament was in session-be it known to the members of this house-which was made without notice to the
public and is an infringement of the rights and privileges of parliament. However, that is in passing.
This bill, I think, should be passed, because it is an evidence that private enterprise is not yet quite dead in relation to civil aviation in this country. It probably is on its way out if the policy of the Minister of Transport is carried to its logical conclusion. I should like to see this bill go to the railway committee, and there the promoters will of course appear to support their proposals and tell the people of Canada just what they have in mind. I think I know what they have in mind. They desire to get a corporate franchise and, if possible, to get authorization to operate certain routes in the maritime provinces; routes, it may be, which have been denied to other private enterprise; I do not know about that. The people who are behind this measure are quite capable financially of entering into this class of transportation business.
I merely rose for the purpose of saying that this bill would have been unnecessary if there had not been an invasion of parliamentary rights on the part of the ministry, and, second, that if these people mean business in the future they should be given encouragement, but if they only mean to get a franchise which will have a nuisance value in the future, it ought not to be granted.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wonder whether any member of the government would care to indicate whether the passing of this bill will in any way conflict with the policies proposed by the government in connection with civil aviation. speechtext:
I did not

You generally leave out what you want to say and say what you do not want to say.

This granting of charters to air lines takes me back over the history of Canada a few years ago when we were granting charters to those engaged in the railway enterprise. What was the outcome? maintopic: PATENT APPLICATION OP CLAUDE H. PETERS

speechtext: Mr. G. J. McILRAlTH (Ottawa West) moved the second reading of bill No. 94, respecting a certain patent application of Claude II. Peters.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PATENT APPLICATION OP CLAUDE H. PETERS
speechtext:
By way of interrogation rather than to make any remarks, may I ask the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill whether, to his knowledge, there are any precedents along the line suggested in the bill itself? It opens up an avenue which perhaps may have been opened before. If my memory is correct, and I think it is, when the hon. gentleman introduced the bill he stated that a firm of solicitors was in default with respect to the patent application mentioned in the bill. On a question put to him, as to whether or not the firm of solicitors had been struck from the record because of this particular default, I believe he said it was so. It would appear on the surface as though equity would
Patent Application

be done if this bill were passed and the applicant put in the same position as he was in relation to the original application, so as to wipe out any injustice that might have occurred through no fault of his own. Perhaps the hon. member when, he closes the debate will answer the question as to whether or not this will be creating a precedent, because after all this is an important matter.

maintopic: PATENT APPLICATION OP CLAUDE H. PETERS
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition is quite correct. He deals with the causes that make this bill necessary. It was a firm of patent attorneys, not solicitors, that was in default. The practice under the Patent Act is to set up a registry, and all patent attorneys entitled to practise under that act are registered. By reason of the failure on the part of the firm to which the applicant sent his work, to carry out its duties this bill becomes necessary.
With respect to the question of precedent, I regret I am not able to answer the question asked by the leader of the opposition, but I shall have the information when the bill is in committee. I would point out, however, that even with the bill the applicant is not in as good position as he would have been had the patent attorneys not neglected their duties. It might be pointed out that under the provisions of the bill the rights of other persons which have arisen since the date his patent would normally have been dealt with are fully protected. We do not know what rights may have arisen in the meantime, but any rights that have arisen are protected under the bill as proposed. Therefore, in no circumstances can the applicant be in as good position as he would have been had he not employed this particular firm of Canadian patent attorneys. As was stated by the leader of the opposition, we are considering this bill because of the failure of the firm of patent attorneys to carry out its duties.

maintopic: PATENT APPLICATION OP CLAUDE H. PETERS
speechtext:
Perhaps with the consent of the house I might make just one observation with respect to that. By giving second reading to this bill and referring it to the appropriate committee. I hope we shall not be setting up a precedent so that in subsequent sessions we shall be asked to take similar action when an agent or a person who is employed by some other person, whether he be a patent attorney, a solicitor, or under whatever name he may be known, defaults in his duties. I hope it will be recognized that this parliament will have no obligation either morally, legally or constitutionally to make good in the future default to the person who employed the defaulter to act for him. That is the only point with respect to this bill that seems to present itself. This is the first time

since I have been in the House of Commons that parliament has been asked to act in such a way. While it is true we are dealing with this individual application at the present time and that we should as a parliament attempt, if possible, to rectify what seems to be a glaring piece of injustice, and one which was wdiolly beyond the power and control of the aggrieved person, yet, I do hope it will be made abundantly clear both in committee and on third reading of the bill that parliament is not creating a precedent whereby agencies and defaulters of this kind can have their mistakes corrected. After all, we must remember it was not this parliament nor this government nor the committee which deals with it that had anything to do with the choosing of the particular agent, solicitor or attorney employed by this man to carry out his orders. I hope that will be distinctly understood. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I have encroached upon the time of the house to this extent, but I thought it was important in view of the explanation which the hon. member has made.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the second time and referred to the committee on miscellaneous private bills.
Mr. J. H. BLACKMORE (Lethbridge) moved the second reading of bill No. 109 respecting the Alberta Provincial Bank.
I understood the mover of second reading of this bill was in a position to explain its contents.

It is the settled conviction of the people of Alberta that the various provinces in the dominion should be permitted to have provincial banks. They believe that had that policy been followed from the beginning, the economy of Canada would have been in a far better conditon than it is now. The Alberta government is simply petitioning the dominion government for authority to establish a provincial bank for Alberta.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot, on behalf of the government, consent to the second reading of this bill. I will, however, propose that the course that was taken in 1940 with respect to a similar bill be taken in regard to this bill, namely, that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce for consideration and report.
I must, I think, give some reasons why I think that is the proper course to follow. I

Alberta Provincial Bank
have looked at the bill and I have also examined the bill which was introduced in the Alberta legislature authorizing the formation of the Alberta provincial bank. I have not seen the act which was passed by the Alberta legislature, and I do not know whether the act is in the same terms as the bill that was introduced; but the plan' of the Alberta government is to establish a bank called the Alberta provincial bank and that the owners of that bank will be province of Alberta. The $500,000 which are initially subscribed for shares are to be paid by the government of Alberta. It is to be Alberta provincial money. The directors of the bank are the members of the Alberta provincial government. The directors are not to own shares in their own right, as provided by the Bank Act, but are to hold their shares in trust for the province of Alberta.
Then by section 5 of the bill it is proposed that some sixteen sections of the Bank Act shall not apply to the proposed new Alberta provincial bank. Let me refer to a few of these sections. In proposing that sections 11 and 20 of the Bank Act shall not apply, certain minimum requirements are removed in the matter of both provisional directors and the directors who are elected by the shareholders. These two sections require that each provisional director or elected director be (1) a bona fide subscriber of stock of the bank on his own behalf; (2) become the absolute and sole owner in his individual right of such stock, and not as trustee or in the right of another; (3) a subscriber for and pay up not less than $3,000 for such stock in the case of a bank capitalized at $1,000,000 or less, $4,000 in the case of a bank capitalized at over $1,000,000 but not over $3,000,000, and $5,000 in the case of a bank capitalized at over $3,000,000. A further requirement in the case of directors elected by the shareholders is that a majority shall be natural born or naturalized British subjects domiciled in Canada. This bill dispenses with these minimum requirements of the Bank Act, and id doing so the bill would appear to be running contrary to a fundamental principle of that act, which is that bank directors be not mere trustees or nominees of some unknown or impersonal owner of stock, but that they be individuals with a definite personal stake in the business and a personal responsibility for the way in which the affairs of the bank are conducted and the money of the depositors is handled. I referred to the provision of the Bank Act which ensures that a majority of the elected directors must be British subjects domiciled in Canada. This provision is put there for a purpose. Any exclusion of its operation in the 100-184
case of a particular bank would seem to require the most careful consideration by this parliament.
Then section 12 of the Bank Act is not to apply to the proposed bank. This' section provides for the opening of stock books for public subscription after ten days' public notice. A subscriber to stock is required to give particulars of his address and occupation as well as the number of shares subscribed for. Section 33 of the Bank Act is excluded. This section provides that any of the original unsubscribed stock or any increase in stock may be allotted to the original subscribers pro rata at not less than par and, inter alia, for a price payable in money. These safeguards are of the utmost importance to depositors and creditors of a bank. Any exception from the operation of this section should be most carefully considered. In excluding sections 35, 37, 39, 40 and 41 of the Bank Act, the bill removes provisions dealing with the right to call on shareholders to pay up any unpaid amount on their stock. It may be that the committee or this house, after examining the Alberta statute, will come to the conclusion that these sections of the Bank Act have no application in this particular case. On the other hand, parliament may come to the conclusion that the dominion should not enact legislation leaving this matter unprotected and dependent upon the continuation of the present provincial legislation.
The other sections of the Bank Act which are excluded have to do with the transfer and transmission of the shares in a bank. These exclusions have to be examined in the light of the provincial statute, which contemplates a holding of the shares by members of the government of the province, and the cessation of their ownership of the shares when they cease to be members of the government of the province. Here also the question of the continuation of the provincial statute in its present form must be examined. In pith and substance the bill is just what the mover described it to be; it is a bill to make the province of Alberta a bank.
Another department of the government.
It is to give the province of Alberta power to have a provincial bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends upon what you call a province, but it makes the provincial government of Alberta a bank.

Do you call the government of the Dominion of Canada a bank in the case of the Bank of Canada?

Alberta Provincial Bank

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Certainly not. The Bank of Canada is a national bank, and the proposed bank will be a provincial bank. To say that the provincial government will be a bank is just as absurd as to say that the dominion government is a bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But the directors of this proposed bank are to be the ministers of the crown in the province of Alberta. Apparently the whole intention is that these ministers will sit in their executive council chamber one hour, and then go on with the business of the bank. It is the executive council of the province of Alberta functioning as a bank. That was the conclusion of the law officers of the crown with regard to the previous bills introduced to incorporate an Alberta provincial bank, which were submitted to this parliament in 1940 and 1941. On those two occasions the law officers of the crown expressed grave doubts as to the constitutional validity of such a proposal. They have not had an opportunity to give full consideration to bill No. 109 and to the recently enacted Alberta statute, which has a bearing on the question of constitutionality. The terms of that provincial statute would, of course, have a bearing on that question.
Again, until the amendments to the Bank Act have been passed by this parliament, it would not be advisable to give this bill second reading. In bill No. 91, which has just been referred to the banking and commerce committee, the right to issue notes is to be taken away from existing banks as from January 1, 1945, and is to be denied to new banks. The double liability feature of the bank stock is to be amended in accordance with such changes. In reading bill No. 109, I take it that the sponsors had such amendments to the Bank Act in mind, because there is no provision for any liability in addition to the original 8500,000. That might not make much difference if the amendments to the Bank Act introduced this year become law, but one never knows whether or not they will become law. If they do not become law perhaps this bill should be changed somewhat, if, indeed, it is considered at all.
For these reasons, because this experiment is something never contemplated by the Bank Act; because it excludes the operation of quite a number of important sections, and because its constitutional validity is at least doubtful, I should think there would be something pretty anomalous about making a provincial government a bank, or a province a bank, to all intents and purposes. That is what this does; it puts them in the banking business.
No more than the dominion cabinet is a bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are on the constitutional point now, and constitutionally this is a dominion sphere, not a provincial sphere.

That is why we are
asking the dominion to give us power to have a bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question is whether we
have power to delegate that; that is the constitutional point I am talking about. Therefore for these reasons-and possibly there are other reasons as well-I wish to move in amendment:
That this ibill be not now read a second time, tout that the subject matter thereof be referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce for consideration and report.
Mr. Speaker, if my memory serves me correctly, that was the course pursued on a previous occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The bill
was not read a second time, but was referred to the banking committee for consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

And it is
my recollection that on that occasion I took the position that this house might as well deal with the principle of the bill right here and now, without its going to the committee.
The minister's observations opposing a second reading of the bill have a good deal of weight; there is m>
doubt about that. A grave constitutional principle is at stake. I do not think it is within the powers of parliament to delegate to a province the jurisdictional functions of the federal government, which are comprised within the provisions of section 91 of the British North America Act- and especially in the form in which it is proposed to be done here.
I should have thought the straightforward course would be to deal with the principle of the bill now, under this motion. However, since the ministry is apparently not prepared to do that-although that would be the courageous course, and the course which I think will be followed in the end-I am not going to oppose the amendment. I should think, though, that we might as well deal with this question as it now presents itself to the house in the matter of the principle involved in this proposed legislation. The house has to grapple with this situation sooner or later, and sending

Alberta Provincial Bank
it to a committee which already promises to be more than overworked will not ensure for it any better consideration.
I am not going to state any opinion I hold with respect to the proposal, but I suggest it would be much better to deal with the matter here and now, once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has said, the house must grapple with this situation sooner or later. But the way in which the house should grapple with it is not, in my judgment, the way in which the hon. member for York-Sunbury has in mind.
If it is not constitutionally competent for the dominion government to grant to a provincial government the right to have a bank, then something was seriously wrong with the constitution of Canada when it was framed.
That is a matter of opinion.

To tell any sensible individual, anywhere, that the province of Ontario, for example, is not entitled to have a provincial bank, is to say something that commends itself to any ordinary intelligence as being absurd. And to say that this dominion parliament, which is a creature of the various provincial legislatures of this country-[DOT]
Well, that is a new theory of confederation.

To say that this parliament, which is the creature of the four original provinces of the dominion, has not the power to give back to one of those provinces the right to have a bank, is to say something that would puzzle the traditional Philadelphia lawyer.
I maintain that the time has come when the house has to face the responsibility of granting to the provinces the right to have banks. Alberta is merely leading the way. Her vision is clear; she knows where she wants to go, and she knows where she will go if the reactionaries who stand in the way of progress in this nation do not block her. The question is clear: Is this parliament going to give a sovereign province of the dominion the power to have some little influence in the conduct of the economy of that province, or is it not? I maintain that it is the duty of this parliament to grant a province of the dominion the right to have a bank.
The minister had several objections. Those objections are caused from the fact that there is an anomalous situation in the dominion.
100-184i
When the constitution of Canada was framed, apparently no provision was made for the granting of a bank to any province, in case such province should wish to have a bank. The result is that new ground has to be broken. Alberta, with the advice of an exceedingly well-informed attorney general's staff, has devised a scheme which, in their judgment, constitutes the best scheme for granting a bank to a province. This would constitute a precedent under which other provinces of the dominion in their turn could be granted banks.
I believe I have said sufficient to justify the house in voting down the minister's amendment, and voting for the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I was not quite satisfied with the minister's explanation that this parliament cannot constitutionally give a province the right to set up a bank. I am wondering just how it was that parliament was able to grant to private individuals the right to set up banks-a right that the dominion cannot grant to a province.
I understand that the control of credit and finance was, by the British North America Act, vested in the dominion government; and that shortly after confederation the dominion government did delegate that privilege to banks. I am wondering just what the difference is between that concession to the banks, and the concession here asked.
The minister pointed out further in his speech that certain sections of the Bank Act shall not apply. I realize that I may not ask a question at this point, but possibly the minister will clear up the situation I am wondering whether these same sections now apply to the Bank of Canada, as they do to the private banks; or is the Bank of Canada exempt from the application of some of those sections, as is requested in this bill?
