speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Administration of the defence of Canada regulations, $30,000.

I should like to
revert for a moment to the subject of Jehovah's Witnesses. I realize, from the correspondence and the interviews I have had both with and on behalf of these people, something of the difficulty which confronts the government, and particularly those departments of the government concerned with selective service and national defence, in dealing with them. I am sure that every hon. member will support the government in its position *that no single group of citizens should, because of their religious beliefs, be exonerated from bearing their share of responsibility as citizens in times such as these.
I am not sure, however, that all the difficulties which have been encountered in dealing with these people are of their own making. The minister intimated that there are government officials who are a bit overzealous. From what I have seen I have been led to believe that many of these officials are. more concerned with the enforcement of regulations for the sake of enforcing them than with the ultimate effect of enforcement upon our war effort.
The minister gave reasons for not lifting the ban on the subsidiary corporations of the Witnesses. My information is that Canada is the only one of the allied countries which places a ban on these corporations. I assume that the United States, and Great Britain and other parts of the empire, are equally concerned for the safety of their particular countries; yet we find that for some reason we alone cannot lift the ban, as recommended by the parliamentary committee some years ago.
I myself am in a bit of a quandary on this point. Reference was made this afternoon to literature which is banned from this country because it is published by the Watch Tower Bible Tract Society of the United States. I, unfortunately perhaps, have in my .possession a book which was published by that society. It is the King James version of the bible. It was left with me a couple of weeks ago by one of these gentlemen who was visiting members

War Appropriation-Justice
of parliament. At the time I did not realize that the book was banned and I took it. My question is, what am I to do with it now? If I keep it I am no longer a law-abiding citizen; I have in my possesion banned literature. If I give it to someone else I am placing that person in the position I now am in. My religious scruples will not permit me to destroy this book, even though I am not a member of Jehovah's Witnesses. I should like the minister to tell me how I stand in this respect with the Department of Justice.
Did the hon. member not previously own a copy?

Wait till I have
finished-
I am astonished.
I did not previously own a copy published by the Bible Tract Society.
I am speaking of the bible.

The minister referred to the large number of these people who profess to be clergymen and therefore claim exemption from military service. Here again, I suppose that all of us will agree with the minister that everyone who professes to be ordained by God and thereby claims exemption from military service should not get that exemption. My information is, however, that although these people are reputed to have some thirty thousand members in Canada they are not permitted exemption for a single one of their leaders, although many of them have devoted years of their lives to the full-time work of teaching their doctrines. In this respect too, I understand, Canada is the only one of the allied nations that refuses to grant to those recognized leaders who devote full time to this work exemption on the same ground as is valid for clergymen of other religious denominations.
I have before me the regulations which are in effect in the country of our neighbour to the south, where a considerable number who are able to show that they have been devoting full time to this work are granted exemptions as clergymen. What I should like the minister to explain is, what are the conditions in Canada which make us different from other parts of the empire and the United States and render it impossible for us to grant concessions which these countries have granted?

I was not satisfied with the explanation given by the minister regarding the release of Farr, Lorimer and Schneider from internment. I watched the activities of
Farr and Lorimer in Toronto. Lorimer was a dangerous man. Although not officially the leader, he gave instructions to Farr, who was the organizer. Lorimer was the power behind the throne, the man who pulled the strings. Very often Adrien Arcand used to come to Toronto and, instead of discussing important matters with Farr, would discuss them with Lorimer. When the gang, eleven of them, were taken, they went into custody with the hope that they would be out soon. In the camp Arcand told his people, "Six months, and we shall be.in power in Ottawa."
When things did not go so well with them, in other words, when Hitler was not doing so well, they naturally started to fight among themselves. This is what happened, and Farr weakened. I know of differences that arose between Farr and Adrien Arcand in Fredericton. I brought the matter to the attention of the authorities and pointed out that Farr was weakening, but not so Lorimer. Lorimer was in the camp very close to the nazis. At all times he lined himself up with the German nazis against anyone who dared to utter a word against fascism or nazism. I cannot understand, therefore, why Lorimer was released even earlier than Farr. If Farr weakened, it was not because he lost faith in the ideals of fascism and became a great upholder of democracy, but because the ship was sinking and the rat was willing to jump off the ship.
I cannot understand why men like these
should be released. We are told that the situation to-day is better in regard to the war and that we can give these people a chance.
Can you understand why Tim Buck was released?

Let me finish. But the nazis, I understand, who are in the camps to-day are as cocky as ever, and if anyone in a camp raises his voice to utter any doubt about the outcome of the war things are made hot for him. I have heard stories of persons-their own people-being practically crippled because they dared to raise their voices and to express a doubt about the ultimate victorj' of Hitler. Why should we imagine that, because one of them says that from now on he will be a good man, he meant it? Can we believe that Schneider has suddenly become a good democrat? It pays him to say so and he says it. I repeat, the nazis are pretty cocky and the fascists have not given up their ideas. When we hear reports of some of the nazis already preparing a great underground movement for the post-war period we can believe it.
War Appropriation-Justice

I do not believe in the theory of softness toward them. If we show softness toward our own native fascists I am very much afraid we shall show it toward the nazi enemies against whom we are fighting at the present time. It is a problem of softness; that is what it is, and I cannot agree that we can afford to be soft with these people.
When these men were arrested, the late Minister of Justice, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, said that the attorney general of Quebec had sent him a report in the matter- I quote from Hansard of the session of 1940 at page 983:
The attorney general of Quebec has sent me a report in the matter, accompanied by certain exhibits which show clearly that those people had communications and intelligence with enemies-Germany, Italy and elsewhere.
If that were true in 1940, how can we in this stage of the war, when the toughest battles are being fought, release these people? At the same time the late Minister of Justice, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) as to whether there would be a trial for these people, said, "Yes, there will be a trial." I would say that there should have been a trial. If these people were guilty of treason, the people of Canada should have known about it and no one would have been deceived. Trials are taking place in the United States at the present time. There are thirty seditionists appearing for trial there. The whole story will be told to the American people and their morale will be strengthened rather than weakened by the disclosures of the facts. I do not see why people like Arcand and his friends should not have been tried. On March 8, in Washington, in connection with one of the trials taking place there, the attorney general said: " Hitler had his quislings in the various countries. He had a Quisling in Norway, Laval in France, and he had Adrien Arcand in Canada." That is what the attorney general of the United States says; and News Week of this week suggests that after the release of Farr and Lorimer there is talk of the release of Adrien Arcand. If that were to happen, then I say it would be a crime against the people of Canada. I will go farther and say that we cannot even be satisfied with having taken in the few that we have.
In the province of Quebec, the good name of our people is being besmeared by elements like Menard, who to-day issues a sheet known as Le Bavard, in which he writes a eulogy of Major Scott, one of the fascist leaders, who died in the camp, suggesting that a statue be erected to this great soldier-hero who died in the struggle contre la juiverie, as he describes it-the struggle against Jewry.

Menard was not touched, although he was one of the early editors of Le Goglu and Le Patriote. We have Salluste Lavery, one of the old gang of fascists. He was not touched. There are many others who, by means of their agitation in the province, are issuing material of a type which is calculated to do great harm. The other day I picked up "La Priere d'un Juif", "A Jewish Prayer", the most insulting piece of propaganda ever issued in a democratic country, especially at this time of war. It is unsigned, but surely it should not be very difficult for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Department of Justice, by merely checking the type, to find out where this insulting publication was printed and who was responsible for it.
On the other hand, in regard to certain other elements, the same Department of Justice' is not too lenient. I refer to a group of Finns in Sudbury, editors of a paper known as Vapaus, a paper which has always been opposed to the leadership of the Finnish fascist Mannerheim. It is a paper that upholds Canada's war effort. There are a few people at the head of that paper who have to report every month to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, though I do not know of any other Finns who have to report similarly. One of these people has three sons in the armed forces. Such a situation is ridiculous. I should like to know who advises the Department of Justice in regard to these people. They have always been anti-fascist; they have never had anything to do with Mannerheim or his gang; yet they have to report once every month to the R.C.M.P. It is a most unsatisfactory state of affairs and I should like to have an explanation of the matter.
I wish to ask a few more questions. How does it happen that the R.C.M.P. and the Department of Justice are involved in cases of men who have joined the army? I have here a letter of a man who has been in the army. He was proposed for officer training and was suddenly called in by the personnel man and told, "we like your work very much; you are very good, but in 1939 you were a member of the young communist league and a C I O. organizer. The R.C.M.P. say you cannot go to the officers training school". Who gives the R.C.M.P. that power? Do we not have a military department that looks after those matters or is the R.C.MP. a supergovernment? I should like an answer to that question.
I know a man who wants to go back to Italy. He was a member of the Italian government before Mussolini came into power. He was the mayor of an Italian town. He wants to return to Italy to do his duty to his

War Appropriation-Justice
country, but what happens? The R.C.M.P. tell that man that he cannot return to his own country. I say that is going beyond the duties of the R.C.M.P. and the Department of Justice. I have here a copy of the report of the R.C.M.P. We find a whole section in it on labour, although there is a labour department. What have the R.C.M.P. to do with labour?

Then I shall conclude my remarks. I raise these points not because I want to attack the government or to raise opposition for the sake of opposition, but because the policy of the department appears to me to be a policy that has nothing in common with the policy of the government or the policy of the people fighting against fascism.

It seems to me that we have had a good illustration this evening of what many of us feared would occur when the defence of Canada regulations were first adopted by this government and approved by parliament.
I do not believe that it is ever wise to put people in gaol or to incarcerate them without giving them an opportunity to defend themselves according to the principles of democratic justice. I have a good deal of sympathy with the point of view that we may have put into internment camps people who ought not to have been there, and we may have let out of internment camps people who ought still to be in them. The ruspicions of the people are aroused. They think there has been either persecution of favouritism. There are no public records to show whether there has been persecution or favouritism. To-day we have the statement made-and I believe that the statement is justified-that the person named Lorimer is the man who with Arcand was regarded as the agent of the nazi movement and of Hitler in this country. Many people are suggesting that. I have had letters, as I have no doubt have other hon. members, and resolutions over the past few weeks, stating definitely that the government is more friendly to persons of that type than to persons with democratic sympathies. I do not believe that statement, but I know such statements are being made and believed. To-night we have had an expression of such an opinion. Of course, the defence of Canada regulations are still in effect and we are still operating under them. I remember very well that when they were brought down early in the war we
opposed them, and we have endeavoured to get something in the nature of a proper trial for people who are incarcerated.
I realize, as will all hon. members who have served on the defence of Canada regulations, that there may have been occasions when it might have been almost impossible, because of the war situation and the need of seeing to it that persons who were engaged in subversive activities were not forewarned of the people who were reporting upon them, not to vary to some extent the form of trial with which we have been familiar; but I insist that we have been wrong in this respect. To-day we are raising in the minds of the people across the country the opinion that there is an element of favouritism or undue influence somewhere that is allowing people like the ones we have been discussing this afternoon and this evening to be at liberty without an adequate explanation or without even an adequate trial. I have confidence in some of the people who have headed those committees. Some of us in this house who are aware-as some of us are-of the situation that developed when Italy entered the war, and what happened then, know how dangerous this kind of method of dealing with the problem which confronted the nation can be. I suggest that the minister and the department owe it to the house and the country to give a clear explanation as to why these things are being done at the present time; otherwise the suspicion will continue either that there has been undue poltical influence or that a certain amount of favouritism has been exercised in some of these cases.
I am of the opinion that where you have a man like the person named by the hon. member for Cartier, Lorimer, who was engaged in the kind of activities in which I am told and believe he was engaged, in the early part of the war or before the war, no kind of declaration that he was prepared to act differently would satisfy my mind. I would want some other and more concrete assurances that we would not be subject to the kind of propaganda that these people were engaged in. I know the hon. member for Cartier wrote a very interesting pamphlet a few years ago in which he outlined some of the activities of these people. I remember getting a copy of it at the time. It seems to me that the minister will have to be clear to the committee, and through the committee to the country, as to why these sympathizers with the nazi regime have been let out among us at this particular time.

The minister said this afternoon that there were 300 in internment. He then referred to 120 of British origin in internment. Is the latter figure of 120 included in the 300, or an additional number to be added to it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is included in it.

How many Japanese are now in internment? Would the minister divide the number into those who are Japanese nationals, those who have been naturalized, and those who are Canadian bom?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: As of May 15 there appear to be 430 persons of the Japanese race still interned, of whom 268 were interned under regulation 21, as being British subjects, or treated as such, and of whom 162 were interned under regulation 25 as being Japanese nationals, or treated as such.

Does that include the naturalized ones?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. The 268 include the naturalized ones. I have not the division between those who were treated as British subjects because of naturalization, and those who were treated as such because of birth in this country.

Would it be possible to obtain that figure, and let me have it?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think it will be possible, although it will take some little time. However, I shall be glad to have instructions given to have a statement prepared as accurately as we can have it prepared from the records. Our records are fairly complete. It will take some time, because it will involve looking up the pre-war registrations which, as the hon. member knows, were obtained by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We would have to check the information obtained at that time with the names of the internees dealt with under regulation 21.

Have any Japanese who were once interned been released, as so many of those of Teutonic origin have been released?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The total number of persons of Japanese race who were interned is 782, of whom 352 have been released. The hon. member will recall that in the 782 there are included some who temporarily refused to accept orders of removal issued against them. I have not with me the break-down as to how many were regarded as British subjects, either through naturalization or through being born here. That is the total number of those who were released.
Quite a large number were interned for only a short time because they had refused to comply with the removal orders issued against them. As soon as they did agree to comply with the removal orders they were removed from the internment camps, under the regulations, but came under the supervision of the British Columbia Japanese commission. They were not given full release, but were merely taken out of the internment camps and turned over to those in charge of housing the Japanese who had been removed from the protected area in British Columbia.

Will the minister reply to
the questions asked by the hon. members for Cartier and Rosetown-Biggar in connection with the release of Lorimer? The charge was made that many persons in Canada have the feeling that the minister's department is more sympathetic toward people of fascist tendencies than toward those following the democratic way of life. I think the minister owes it to the committee to reply to that question.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would ask the hon. member, as well as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, to look at the statement I made this afternoon. It is unfortunate that they were not in the chamber at that time and that the matter has been raised again.
I shall be very glad to read what the minister said. After I sat down I found that I had been out of the chamber when the reply was given; I was not aware of that when I spoke.

I was present this afternoon when the minister made his reply and as far as I am concerned it leaves a lot of doubt in my mind. The united nations are beginning to enter a decisive phase of the war and the international picture is somewhat beclouded and complicated from the political point of view. I listened to the minister very carefully and his reply leaves much to be desired. In her statement this afternoon with respect to the release of this man Schneider, the hon. member for North Battleford in effect accused the government of jeopardizing the safety of the state because of political expediency. That was my understanding of her statement, and the minister's reply did not clarify it.
In connection with Lorimer and Farr, the records of these two men are well known to practically every one in Canada who has paid any attention to national affairs. They were recognized as nationally-known fascists. Early in the war they were tried, convicted and interned as enemies of the state. I am calling a spade a spade; that was my conception of it. During their internment they softened up a little., and because of that the committees which retried their cases two or three times accepted their word that they were not going to be bad any more. One of them had received a licking from his friends while he was incarcerated and the other gave his word he would be good.
How much can you depend upon the word of a nazi or fascist? Mussolini and Hitler
War Appropriation-Justice

have demonstrated to the world that their signed or pledged word does not mean a thing except to gain time in order to serve their own ends. This indicates to me that at this stage of the war we are not thinking realistically. The release of Sir Oswald Mosley in England, and the release of nationally and internationally known fascists in Canada at a time like this should1 not have occurred.
I am not the kind of person who thinks anyone who does not agree with me should be interned or put in gaol. We have stood for the principle of a fair trial right through the whole process of discussing the defence of Canada regulations. However, I contend that once a man has had a fair trial, is convicted and sentenced, that sentence should be carried out to its logical conclusion. This is based upon the examination being properly made in the first place. This must 'be done if we are to maintain respect for the laws of the country. If earlier in the war we convicted the men we are discussing to-night of being enemies of the state, they are still enemies of the state. This country is now in a most dangerous stage of the war.
If there ever were a time during the fighting of this war when active nazis or fascists could be effective on the outside, it is the present time when the united nations are taking the offensive. If we are to take this attitude now, what attitude are we to take with international gangsters like Hitler and his satellites? If to-morrow his own people turn against him; if the Russians seem to be getting a little too close and Hitler decides that discretion is the better part of valour, that he should weep on someone's shoulder and throw up his hands, would there be any justification for the united nations withdrawing the slogan of unconditional surrender with which they have been taking the people forward? If we are to deal with the convicted enemies of this country in the way we have been, this trend will develop internationally and we shall lose the objectives for which we are fighting this war just as we lost those for which we fought in the last war.
I heard the minister's statement and I realize that he was depending upon the committees, but in my opinion the release of these three men is sowing discord in the minds of a great many people across this country who are really fighting this war. They are fighting for unconditional surrender and the complete elimination of the philosophy for which our enemies stand. I do not believe that a change of mind can take place overnight. Long before I ever expected to come into this house these people were known to me; I knew their records, their histories and their activities. I was quite satisfied when they were put away, and I

believed that the expiration of their sentences would not take place until the war was over and peace was concluded.
They can then be tried without any war hysteria and the proper punishment meted out. We should not get soft at this time. We should not consider negotiating or dealing with people who are known to be enemies of the state until the main issue on the other side is definitely and finally settled.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police-[DOT]
Salaries, $643,000.

There is quite an increase this year in this first item. However, before asking a question on that may I offer a few words in recognition of the wonderful service which this force has rendered and is rendering to-day to this country. Great credit is due to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the splendid work done by the members of the force during these years of war. When the war began there was no force which received such small recognition in the matter of pay and otherwise as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They still are rather hampered. They have to serve many years before they are allowed to marry, and they forgo many privileges and freedoms in one way and another. They are highly trained and extremely efficient, and the money we vote to expend upon them on behalf of the taxpayers is one of the best investments to which taxes can be put. In the light of the discussion we have had this afternoon, let me say that if there is any body of men to whom we should be grateful because of the small amount of sabotage which has occurred during these war years, it is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I should like the minister to give us some idea of the use to which this extra $100,000 for salaries will be put. Also I would repeat a question which I asked a year ago: in the case of a member of the force who has had meritorious service and a clear record for a period of, say fifteen or twenty years, what recognition does he receive? I think there should be some means of promotion or provision whereby he will receive promotion, or a corresponding financial benefit upon retirement. Is anything like this done or proposed to be done?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am glad to be able to assure the hon. member that we do attempt to give full recognition, because the retirement allowance under the superannuation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police does not follow the ordinary rule of the civil service; it is based upon the pay and allowances being received at the time of retirement. That is one of the factors of calculation; the other is the period of service. The factor which is taken to be multiplied by the years of service
is the pay and allowances at the moment of retirement; and the policy of the commissioner and his assistant commissioners to take care of meritorious service is to make promotions as expeditiously as the retirements in the upper level permit. Since the beginning of the war, because of the urgency of the situation and because the commissioner was authorized to take on 2,500 constable guards and 500 special constables, the releasing of the higher officers upon having attained what might otherwise be the age limits has had to be retarded. It has been necessary to keep in the service all those who were physically able to perform service, and one of the unfortunate incidents of that is that it has slowed up, to some extent, promotions right down through the force. The only hope we have been able to hold out to the men who have not obtained their promotions through the various ranks quite as rapidly as they would have expected to obtain them under normal conditions, is that when the war is over and we are able to dispense with the special men who have been taken on, quite a number of vacancies will occur, and the rapidity of the subsequent promotions will make up for the slowness during the war period.

I should also like to know the reason for the increase of over $100,090 in this first item.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This increase is required for unforeseen outlays in connection with the engagement of clerks, stenographers, typists and employed civilians. The commissioner, as he has to be, is always very prudent; in looking at the sheet which has been distributed the hon. member will see that the provisions in the estimate have always been quite ample; and although it has not been possible, because of the man-power situation, to find with respect, for instance, to pay and allowances, which are the big items here, all the additional constables or special constables authorized by the order in council, the commissioner still provides for salaries and allowances for the full establishment if he can obtain them. Of course, if the situation became urgent, we would obtain them. There have been authorized, for instance, 2,500 constable guards. We have something like 1,800. We could get the additional 700 if the need for them were sufficiently urgent. We would have plenty of use for them if we could use them in all the work which has to be done. But there is some work for which untrained men cannot be used; and the reason for this provision is that we shall have under this war appropriation
War Appropriation-Justice

sufficient to pay the numbers that have been authorized, although we have not yet found it possible to take them all on.
This increase on the civilian side is because the commissioner has been taking on untrained civilians to do work which was being performed by men who were enrolled in the force. We have not a women's division, but we have been taking on civilians to do work which was being done under normal conditions by men who belonged to the regular establishment. The commissioner prefers to take them out of the kind of service that can be done by civilians rather than engage civilians for constable work.

I feel it my duty to bring to the notice of the committee an example of the remarkable skill and ability of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Early last September I was away in a remote part of the Rocky mountains in far western Alberta and I came down the mountain to a place called Rocky Mountain House by train. The train arrived at ten o'clock. I was accompanied by a Mr. Grindly, a member of the Alberta government's engineers, who had been with me in the mountains. We had left our car at the garage on Main street of Rocky Mountain House. As 1 say, the train arrived at the station at ten o'clock, and after getting our car I expressed a wish to go to see Old Rocky Mountain House, three miles away. We drove over town and I asked a man on Main street whether he could direct us to Old Rocky Mountain House. Following his directions, we drove away and came to the Saskatchewan river. We had to ferry over the river. I asked the ferryman the direction to Old Rocky Mountain House and he said that after crossing the river I should turn left and proceed for a mile and a half. We did so. At the same time, I wanted to find the mouth of Clearwater river. I had passed it by on account of the trees. I had not seen it. When I came back I told the ferryman that I had not found the mouth of Clearwater river, and he said, "When you cross the river this time turn to the right on the top of the hill, and the first bridge you come to will be Clearwater river." I did so, and a few moments later, after retracing our steps, as we came down the road, a man driving a car put his hand out of the window beckoning to us to stop. When we came abreast of his car he said he was a mounted policeman and asked "Is there a Mr. MacNicol in your car?" I said, "Yes, there is. I am John R. MacNicol." He said, "There is an important message for you at the railway station." It happened to be a message informing me that a relative had died. He said that they had received instructions to find me wherever I might be. There was an example

of most remarkable ability on the part of the police. How he found me I do not know. I had left the station at ten o'clock, and shortly after the telegram arrived and the mounted police started out to locate me. Within twenty-five minutes he had found me, I will not say in the wilds of Alberta, but in a remote area. I inquired his name, and I believe it was R. A. McMullen. I wish the minister would drop that police official a letter congratulating him upon his ability to find his man, so to speak. As I say, I do not know how he found me. I had not time to ask him, because I hurried to the station to get the wire, and I was speaking to Toronto at ten-fifty-five. They have a skill, intuition and ability that, in my opinion, cannot be surpassed by any police force in the world. They are able to find their man.

Tributes to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are unnecessary. The service they render the country is their own reward.
There is one phase I would take up with the minister, namely, the question of developing the field of forensic medicine. During the past three years there has been developed in Regina a laboratory for the scientific investigation of crime and it has achieved a reputation all over North America. It was founded as a result of the influence of Commissioner Wood. It was placed under the control of the late Doctor Maurice Powers, whose work, I am sure, is known to you, Mr. Chairman, and to all those who appreciate the value of scientific knowledge in relation to crime and its detection.
Doctor Powers met an untimely end during the past, summer while engaged in the service to which he was devoting his life. His work, as I have already stated, was known everywhere on this continent. He developed a laboratory that was unexcelled in this country, and I suggest to the minister that in order to increase and widen the influence of the mounted police encouragement should be given a number of young medical students or medical men to enter the field of forensic medicine and continue the work that was so ably carried on during the all too short lifetime of Doctor Powers.
A further matter which I think I should bring to the attention of the minister was mentioned by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), namely, the regulation that has been in effect for so many years forbidding the marriage of young men in the mounted police until they have served a period of eight years. I have heard numbers of these young men point out that they are devoting themselves to the service of their country, and

War Appropriation-Justice
this regulation, while there may have been meritorious reasons for its existence in former years, is no longer necessary. There is no reason for its continuance beyond the initial three-year period. The removal of that regulation or, in any event, an alteration in it to make it applicable only during the first three years of service would result in the recruitment to the force of many young men who, after the war is over, will desire to continue in a semi-military force, but who feel that to operate under the detriment of inability to marry for a considerable period of years is something they cannot accept. I should like to ascertain from the minister his views on these two matters, both of which I advance with a desire to improve the efficiency of the force, high though it is to-day, in order to ensure that this force in years to come will maintain the high tradition it has achieved in the past, particularly since the beginning of the war, when men of the force, regardless of personal convenience, have made sacrifices which only history itself will be able to record.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The matter which the hon. gentleman has discussed is one in which I felt very much as he does. I discussed it with the commissioner and I was given reasons which appeared to me to be very weighty. The first is that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police cannot afford to have its men incurring debts which they do not regularly pay. Their reputation is such that they must be regarded as good credit risks in the communities in which they five, and it is only after eight years of service that a man can attain the pay of a full constable. Up to the present time, though there has been made within recent months quite a substantial war-time increase in pay, the salaries that are being paid are not sufficient to enable a man to maintain a family until he has reached the time when he receives the constable's wage. That was one reason.
Another reason was that at the present time fifty-eight per cent of the -regular personnel of the R.C.M.P. is made up of married men, and with the tight housing situation that has existed all over the country one of the difficulties of the commissioner has been to find a sufficient number of unmarried qualified constables to do work at places where no housing accommodation for families could be found. I hope that is a temporary situation in this country. I hope it will not always be so that the distribution of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel will depend upon the possible housing conditions in the various localities. But during the war period that has been a serious consideration with which the commissioner has had to wrestle, the possibility of placing in barracks a sufficient number of sufficiently qualified men to maintain the standards of service that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police wish to give to the communities in which they are located. I hope that these are two objections that it will be possible to overcome some day. I hope that some day it will be possible to have the men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police paid, even after only three years of service, a sufficient salary to enable them, like their fellows, to start early the establishment of families. I also hope that it will not be so very long before the acute housing situation can be taken care of and when there will be a sufficient number of the physical things required to make more homes in this country.
The hon. member raised a question with respect to the department which was so ably conducted by Doctor Powers. That is one which is giving us some concern. It has not been possible, notwithstanding applications placed with various medical schools, to find anyone at this time to take over the work that has been inaugurated, and the commissioner has been obliged to resort again to the services, and quite satisfactory services, but not of a permanent nature, of Madame Doctor McGill, the provincial pathologist.
As hon. members know, the distribution of medical practitioners is under the procurement board and the first call on the medical profession, and especially the first call on all those graduating from medical schools, is for the armed forces. It has not yet been possible to find any man who could continue the work started by Doctor Powers. It is the intention of the commissioner not only to try to continue that work but to have it developed, because it is appreciated that it will be of value not only to the reputation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but to the Canadian public in the assistance made available for the administration of justice.

I rise to compliment my hon. friends of the opposition and all hon. members of the committee upon what I regard as practically a unanimous view of the merits and deserts of this great force. I have been privileged to know something of their work, particularly in the first three years of the war, latterly, practically not at all. May I just make one or two observations. First, I would say that if the minister were to be indicted in connection with this item or with his administration of this force it would be because we are not sufficiently recognizing the magnificent service they are rendering, and because we are permitting them to do it still underpaid. I
War Appropriation-Justice

do not know that I could persuade the treasury board that I was right-there we come again to the treasury board. But let me point out this: the qualifications that a young man must have when he enters this force are very, very high. Then the courses that he must follow make it necessary for him to become efficient in ballistics, in the study of chemistry, in horsemanship, in the driving of all types of motor vehicles and in a knowledge of criminal law. AVe do not hear very much of the work they do, but on both oceans they are charged with the duty of searching incoming and outgoing vessels to prevent the possibility of the planning of sabotage, and the record of the lack of any attempts at sabotage in this war is a great tribute to this force.
I think I am entitled to pay a personal tribute to Commissioner General Stuart AVood. He is a man of vast experience, an experience which began many years ago with part-time service in Scotland Yard, that great school of training, where the enemies of crime learn how to combat it. I have concluded my task when I say that I believe this committee can properly be unanimous in a tribute to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a force which has maintained law and order in our country and whose anti-sabotage activities during this war are such that no country in the world can excel.

I am always delighted to see that each year as this particular estimate comes before the committee a certain number of members on all sides of the committee find it fitting and proper to say a few words in praise of this magnificent Canadian organization, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I am particularly pleased with the hon. member for Lake Centre who paid a tribute to the late Doctor Powers. I, too, had the privilege of working with Doctor Powers on a number of cases which happened to come within his particular phase of police activities. I formed the same opinion of Doctor Powers as apparently the hon. member for Lake Centre did. It was a great loss to a new and important branch of police work in Canada when Doctor Powers died. I was concerned when I heard the Minister of Justice say that it has been difficult to find a proper successor to a man whose stamp is placed upon that particular type of work which has been carried on by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I realize, as does the minister, that the first duty of medical students and medical men generally is to the war effort. However, in view of the importance of this work to the whole of Canada, an effort should be made to furnish the mounted

police with the ablest member of the medical profession that can be found to carry on the work of Doctor Powers, for I believe that is absolutely essential if we are to build up a proper establishment.
As I listened to the debate in regard to internments and the other matters arising under the defence of Canada regulations, it struck me, in looking back over the more than four and a half years we have been at war, that this country owes a great debt to the Minister of Justice, whose integrity of purpose has won the respect and confidence of all hon. members and, I am sure, of the great majority of the people of this country. He has had at his right hand one of the finest police bodies in existence to-day, and they have followed the very wisest policy in that type of work. As it is in medicine, so it is in the world of crime; prevention is much better than cure. I have some personal knowledge of the splendid contribution made by the mounted police during this war period in the very field we were discussing to-day, the field of espionage and of subversive elements in our midst. AVhen I consider the few examples that can be brought forward and discussed, which are but the exceptions to the very general rule of freedom in this country from acts of espionage and uncontrolled subversive elements, in my opinion when the story of this work is written it will be found that this police force has discharged its task in an amazingly efficient manner. Therefore I join with the hon. member for Parry Sound and others in urging the minister, his colleagues and the members of this house to recognize the importance of keeping the traditions of this force up to the highest possible standard. This nation will reap a rich reward in the prevention of crime if we can keep the character and morale of the mounted police at a high level. If we look back on the early days in western Canada and the duties then performed by the mounted police, it is easy to realize the allure that service in that force presented. There was the call of adventure to individuals of a very high type. Perhaps that allure has vanished with the more prosaic duties performed by the police in these days, and we must replace it by some other incentive which will maintain the morale of the men. In my opinion the proper incentive is some recognition by way of salary, social standing and anything else we can reasonably do to make service in the force so attractive that the finest young men of this country will make that service their career.
As I say, I merely wish to add my voice to the many that are raised annually in praise and appreciation of the splendid work this force is doing and has done in the past.
MAY i5, 1944
War Appropriation-Justice

I have no desire to enter into any kind of competition in this eulogy to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, so that I shall condense what I think has been meant by everyone who has taken part in this discussion. Having in mind the magnificent job the force has done in this war-time period for such a large number of citizens with such a relatively small number of men; having in mind that they are not very well compensated for their work, I should like to say that in my opinion in the civilian field in this war we can sum it all up as far as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are concerned by saying that never did so few do so much for so many for so little.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In acknowledging the tributes that have been paid to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which all agree are so well deserved, may I ask for one small tribute to the treasury board, which does not receive many tributes. In the month of March I went to the treasury board with a recommendation which contained the following sentence:	"It is estimated that if the
above temporary recommendation is approved the total cost per annum will be approximately 11,242,368.75." The result was a minute of treasury board at once accepting the recommendation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise to join in the tributes that are being paid not to the treasury board but to the men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I am sure the opinion is unanimous that the men of this force deserve the tributes that are paid them annually on the floor of this house. As the minister knows, and as hon. members know, these men have certain grievances, such as those which have been mentioned this evening. Some of us from time to time bring these and other matters to the attention of the. minister or the commissioner of the force; and when we pay our tributes to the services performed by these men we do so in the realization that they give their services loyally and wholeheartedly, despite some of the grievances they hold quite justly. I hope that step by step some of these matters may be adjusted, and that when the war is over, full consideration may be given the claims of these men.
I should like to direct one matter to the attention of the minister and the committee. It suggests that at times the men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are called upon to undertake tasks which are much less heroic, shall I say, than some of the. glamorous things they are called upon to do in the north country or the finding of a member of parliament out in the Rocky mountains.
It seems to me that this particular task which seems to have fallen to the lot of a division of the mounted police is one which this force really ought not to be called upon to perform if it could be avoided. This document was sent to me in the mail; I confess that it was sent anonymously, but it appears to be quite official.
If it is an official document you had better table it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I shall be quite prepared to do so if the leader of the opposition would like it and can find support from the other side of the chamber. It reads:
Canada
Sale by Tender
Tenders addressed to the undersigned will be received at his office at . . .
Then the address is given and a final date. I quote further:
. . . for the following property forfeited under the Excise Act, viz:-Two pairs ladies' rayon stockings, sizes nine and ten. Tenders must be submitted ini sealed envelope marked "Tender". Terms, ten per cent deposit in cash, money order or certified cheque with tender. The highest or any tender not necessarily accepted. Cash on acceptance of tender.
It was posted over the name of the officer commanding a certain division of the force. I am sorry I was not equal to the task of reading this without revealing my sense of amusement, but it did strike me as a sample of the kind of task which is sometimes assigned to mounted police, and which does seem to be a waste of time. Certainly it is very expensive to go through all this rigmarole to sell two pairs of ladies' stockings. Can the minister tell us whether this kind of thing is done very often, or whether this is an exception?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has had more experience with the force than I have, and he tells me he has never known of his force dealing in ladies' stockings.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But there is the document.

Item agreed to.
Construction, $108,000.

Why is there this substantial increase?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This estimate is an extension of the policy which has been instituted, and is for the purpose of dealing with the acute shortage of housing throughout the country. I find that $90,000 is provided here for duplex buildings for married officers. It is
War Appropriation-Justice

estimated that this will be required during the year to take care of the housing of these married officers in various parts of Canada.

Can the minister say where these houses are?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; no definite location can at this time be given as to where it might be necessary to erect these residential buildings. The policy is to lease wherever possible to secure a house. During the dinner hour I approved a recommendation from the commissioner for a house which will be available next August, and which it has been possible to obtain at a rental of S65 a month. On Friday of last week there was a recommendation, in connection with another city, where a house was to become vacant in a few months, and where a lease would be available for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Wherever it is possible to secure quarters on lease, no construction will be done, because we also have to get priorities from those who control supplies, and we have to be able to convince them that it is absolutely necessary, and that we cannot get along without it.

Item agreed to.
Security service, $249,975.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I notice that in paragraph (b) at the bottom of the sheet we have been given we find an explanation for the unexpended balance of last year. The reason given is as follows:
The anticipated general organization of security service being found not necessary.
Perhaps the minister would explain why, in view of that statement, a vote more than twice as large as the amount expended last year should now be asked.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: A large project of security service had been recommended by United Kingdom security officers. Provision had been made for the organization of that service here. I must say that from the outset the commissioner was not very sympathetic to the idea of organizing a new service, and seemed to prefer to have as much of that security work done by his regular staff as might be possible. The man-power situation made it difficult to organize any large special service, and the amount expended in the last fiscal year was expended principally in the ports on the Atlantic coast.
The reason for estimating a possible expenditure of something more than twice the size of the amount expended last year is that there

is always the possibility of having to duplicate on the Pacific coast the security services that have been in operation during the last year on the Atlantic coast.
As the hon. member will notice, these provisions are made in such a way that there will not be any undue delay as to such things as may have to be done in the course of the year. But the hon. member may be assured that none of this money which does not have to be spent will be spent under the direction of the commissioner. It is because of the possibility during the present fiscal year of having to duplicate on the Pacific coast the much smaller security body that has been set up on the Atlantic coast-much smaller than had been first recommended-that this amount is provided.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have one further question growing out of the fact that last year there was an unexpended balance in this item. Hon. members will notice there were similar unexpended balances in respect of other items on this sheet. At the bottom of the page we find this note:
Minus sign under unexpended balance column represents overdrafts in allotments which are to be covered by transfers from balances available in other allotments.
If I understand the procedure correctly, the transferring of a credit from one allotment in order to cover a deficit in another would not be permitted as far as civil estimates are concerned. It must be permissible here, or I am sure the Minister of Justice would not allow it to be done. If that is the case, I just emphasize the fact that what we are dealing with in this committee is not a schedule of specific items but a total amount of money. In dealing with it in that way, we are called upon to give the departments of government considerable latitude for adjusting the different portions of that amount after parliament has passed the bill.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The schedule I have placed before hon. members will not make it possible for the Department of Justice or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to make these expenditures without obtaining specific allocations from the treasury board. There has to be a requisition to treasury board and an allocation by treasury board out of the war appropriation which, as the hon. member has said, is voted as a total amount.

the treasury board would not grant to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police a total amount for the year greater than S6,557.871?
